content:
🔥 take - "Build vs. buy" is a false dichotomy.

It's one of those phrases that sounds clean and strategic in a meeting but falls apart the second you zoom into what "build" actually means.

Because "build" is never just build.

It's build AND maintain AND debug AND document AND scale AND staff AND context-switch your engineering (or vibe coding!) team away from the core product they're supposed to be building and selling.

That last one is the one people miss most.

Every internal tool you build doesn't just cost technical hours. 

It costs focus. 

Your technical team is now supporting an internal product that is not revenue generating, won't be seen by your customers, and will constantly compete for attention with the core service your company actually does.

BUT, I'm not saying build is always wrong. For some use cases and some teams, it's the right call. Typically when the cost to maintain + need for innovation is low – OR for agencies who's core offering is a "service" that you can build custom systems to power the *whole business* through. 

But the mental model of "build vs. buy" makes it sound like a 50/50 coin flip. 

In reality the equation looks more like:

Build + *maintain* + *debug* + *hire for* + *distract from core offering*

VS.

Buy.

The question isn't "can we build this?"

The question is "*SHOULD* we build this?"

"Is our cost + opportunity cost of doing so worth the squeeze? (ROI)"

content:
Had a blast on How I AI with Claire Vo this week talking about how I use AI to manage the chaos of 100-200+ daily Slacks..

But the thing I keep coming back to from our conversation is this:

There are two ways to use AI that I think most people conflate.

1. You can use AI to do a task for you — categorize things, summarize things, draft a response.

OR 

2. You can use AI to build a tool that does something deterministic — code, API calls, structured systems.

They look similar on the surface but they're fundamentally different.

When I built my custom Slack digest, 95% of it is deterministic code. It pulls my notifications via the Slack API, groups them by DMs, threads, group mentions, and direct @-mentions, and pushes them into a kanban-style dashboard. 

🔴 Red for action required. 
🟡 Yellow for need to read.
🟢 Green for FYI.

The only place AI is actively used in a repeated is for categorizing which bucket each message belongs in. Everything else is just ... code. Built with the help of AI, but running deterministically.

And that distinction matters because I see a lot of people trying to get AI to be the system when they should be using AI to build the system.

AI is an incredible builder. It's a less reliable operator. 

So my advice: before you ask AI to do something, ask yourself — should AI be doing this repeatedly, or should AI help me build something that does it reliably every time?

Someone asked me this at Clay Club London last night.

Being an expert in one AI tool but unable to learn the next one at speed is a liability, not an asset.

This is hard even *just* for Clay, not to mention all the other GTM tools out there that you should be knowledgeable at, 

Nassim Taleb has a word for things that break under volatility: Fragile.
AI skills are fragile. They shatter the moment the landscape shifts.

What's antifragile are mindsets — ways of being that get stronger with rapid change.

Curiosity. Agency. Creativity. Care.

Antifragile people thrive in disruption They're more empowered by it.

Stop screening for tools. Start screening for the kind of person who'll master whatever tool comes next.

content:
Something I've been saying a lot recently: 

"I'm playing checkers, you're playing 3D chess."

I use this phrase to mean something specific: everything I'm saying to you is everything I mean. There's no hidden layer. No subtext. No political maneuvering behind the scenes that you need to decode.

Often, the natural instinct at work (and personally) — especially as you gain experience — is to assume 3D chess is being played around you. That there are things being unsaid. Things being kept from you. Things you're supposed to read between the lines on.

And honestly, sometimes it's true. Organizational politics are real.

But in almost every scenario I've come across - it's far easier for everyone involved to put the politics aside and get straight to the point. 

Because playing 3D chess is exhausting, and it zaps energy and time from what really matters most: doing the work. 

3D chess creates a constant background hum of "what did they really mean by that?" 

It erodes trust slowly enough that you don't notice until it's gone.

So I make it a point to tell everyone I work with exactly what's on my mind and how I feel about it. And if I can't say something — I'm explicit about that too, and explicit about why.

"I can't share the details on this yet because it isn't all finalized, but here's what I can tell you."

That sentence alone eliminates more anxiety than any amount of reassurance.

The irony? The more you play checkers internally — straight talk, no hidden moves, full transparency with your team — the better equipped you are to play the 3D chess that you might need externally.

Save the strategy for the competition. Play checkers with your people.

content:
I've been thinking about the traits that make someone a high performer.

Some of the most important ones are counterintuitive.

A few that stand out:

1. High-performers flag when something isn't working — fast.

There's a temptation to white-knuckle it when things go off track. "I can get it back on track. I can get it back on track." You keep telling yourself that story because asking for help feels like admitting defeat.

It's not. It's putting the team ahead of your ego. The best people I've worked with don't wait until a fire is burning to raise their hand. They raise it at the first sign of smoke.

2. They delegate — and not the grunt work.

We have this perception that doing all the work ourselves earns us the right to claim success. But people don't really care whether not *you* did the thing. They care whether or not the thing got *done* — and whether it got *done well*.

Some nuance: you can't just dump busy work on your colleagues. That's not delegation, that's offloading. Real delegation means handing off the parts of your job where someone else has a genuine strength you don't.

Which leads me to ... 

3. They know their weaknesses as well as their strengths.

I love the CliftonStrengths philosophy: your strengths grow infinitely, but everything else grows in a limited capacity. You have maybe 5-10 top strengths out of 34. 

The winning strategy *isn't* to work hard on the other 24. It's to find people whose strengths complement yours.

One that hits home for me recently — admitting I'm not amazing at recruiting. I just so deeply believe in people's potential that I get over excited.

But Varun Anand, IMO, is world-class at this. He sees things in candidates that I can't put words to because it's one of his natural strengths, and it's not mine. 

Some of that is process I can (and continue to!) learn from him. Some of it is intuition I probably never will.

Which is why I love that we work on a team together. I get to lean on Varun for the things he'll always be better at. He gets to lean on me for mine.

Last but not least ... 

4. They don't follow instructions.

This one *sounds* wrong. But the highest performers I've worked with don't listen to what I say — they listen to the *essence* of what I'm saying. They think like owners. They take my suggestions, sit with them, and oftentimes come back with something completely different — and the reasoning to back it up.

When people are thinking at the same level of strategy that you are – "management" feels much more like "collaboration". Which is magical in both directions.

p.s - yes, these are all lessons I have learned the *hard* way myself over my last 3 years at Clay 🤣 I silently failed, was horrible at giving up my legos, reticent to cop to my weaknesses, and trying to do "what I was told" - and in the process - missing the forest for the trees

content:
Something that's been on my mind lately: 
the most important part of sany conversations is what's *not* said.

We spend so much energy on our words. Choosing the right ones. Saying more. Saying it better. Saying it louder.

But the best communicators I've met are masters of the space *between*.

Think about tension for a second.

Every great movie understands this. The scene in The Godfather where Michael sits in the restaurant, silent, while the tension builds before he makes the decision that changes everything. Tarantino's entire career is built on conversations that feel like they're about nothing — until you realize the silence between the words is where the threat lives.

Every great song understands this. The pause before the beat drops. The breath Adele takes before the chorus of Someone Like You. That silence is worth a thousand words. 

*Tension* is the engine of all meaningful work. Tension isn't created by talking *more*. It's created by knowing when to *stop*.

The same thing is true in conversation.

The pause before someone answers often tells you more than the answer itself. The question someone almost asked but didn't. 
The topic that keeps getting circled around but never landed on.

That's where the real communication lives.

We're trained to fill silence. In meetings, in 1:1s, in pitches. Silence feels like failure. Like someone dropped the ball.

But some of the most profound moments of understanding I've experienced happened in quiet. 

A look across the room. 
A beat of stillness after something honest was said. 
The decision to not respond right away because the other person needed the space more than you needed to fill it.

Great design works this way too — whitespace isn't empty. It's what gives everything else meaning.

Next time you're having a serious conversation or giving a presentation - take a moment to pause and ask yourself how you might better play with the tension at hand.

content:
We grew Clay from $1–100M ARR in 2 years. Here are the 4 pillars of the marketing strategy we implemented last year:

Context: As a PLG-heavy company, our challenge when layering SLG was clear—how do you grow both motions? PLG typically attracts SMBs, while SLG serves mid-market and enterprise. Different audiences, personas, and use cases.

At the start of 2025, our Marketing team was ~8 FTE. Prioritization and clarity were non-negotiable. Here we go:

1. PRIORITIZE AUDIENCES WITH PULL EFFECTS

Clay serves multiple segments: service providers, startups, and mid-market/enterprise. With a small team, focus matters.

We prioritized GTM Ops professionals in mid-market tech. Our hypothesis: this audience creates pull. Agencies aspire to serve them, and startups aspire to become them. Both want to follow their best practices.

2. GET OTHERS TO TALK ABOUT US

Our ecosystem is our core distribution advantage.

In marketing, what others say about you matters more than what you say about yourself. We identified the most respected partners in the GTM Ops space—starting with our ecosystem, then expanding to industry leaders.

End users are tactical and live in communities. We mapped key ops communities and built genuine relationships.

Executive buyers (CROs) are different. They’re inundated and operate in closed circles. To break through, we partnered with people they respect—investors and operators they already want to learn from.

3. LESS IS NOT MORE. MORE IS MORE.

Focus and partners aren’t enough if you show up occasionally.

We needed consistent, high-frequency presence. Prospects should feel like we’re everywhere. This meant weekly team alignment around release marketing: what shipped, what’s next. “More is more” became a mantra.

4. MAKE PEOPLE FEEL SPECIAL

Our partner ecosystem is core and must be nurtured.

We obsessed over community milestones—from joining our partner program to major life moments. We aim to surprise and delight because we genuinely care.

Lastly, startups are chaotic by nature. Things will feel overwhelming. If it doesn’t feel chaotic, you’re probably not moving fast enough

content:
Prompting AI is an audit of your own thinking. Most people are failing it.

(p.s - Sophie Alpert elucidated this beautifully in a now viral AI company writing policy, check it out)

In a pre-AI world, every vague instruction, every edge case you didn't consider, every step you hand-waved past — was a failure point. It's impossible to hide lazy thinking from a system that executes *exactly* what you specified.

*With* AI, you can mask lazy thinking. Because AI will give you *some* directionally correct answer to your prompt. And now, you've passed the burden of rigorous thinking onto the person after you – while simply giving them more to process. 

Lazy writing has *always* been lazy thinking. AI doesn't change that equation.

That's my thesis statement for Every's new project — 100 builders predicting what great human work looks like after automation.

My prediction: when agents handle execution, human work collapses into specification.

The old barrier to systems thinking was code. You had to learn to speak the language of computers and navigate machine environments.

That's quickly disappearing — plain English allows us to work with computers in ways we've never been able to before. 

But what *didn't go anywhere* is everything underneath: first-principles decomposition, MECE strategy, knowing what a machine can infer and what it can't.

Engineers already had this habit of mind. It's why teams write specs before touching code.

But with *everyone* now able to *work* like engineers, the biggest gap is going to be teaching people how to *think* like engineers. 

Read my thesis + everyone else's: https://lnkd.in/gNGXh67r

content:
Your reps are doing homework that a machine should be doing for them.

Every time a new lead comes in, someone has to look them up. LinkedIn stalk. Check the company. Google the domain. Figure out if they're worth a call.

Not to mention that all of that takes a *lot* of time! 

And we know speed to lead matters. 

Follow up in < 1 minute and your chances of getting a response go up *391%*. 

That's a lot of missed opportunities that you're spending a lot of human energy and time on. 

We flipped that at Clay.

Now, when a lead comes in — from any source — the research happens automatically before a human ever touches it. 

From a SINGLE email address, our Clay workflow identifies the person, enriches the company, scores the fit, and routes the lead to the right rep. A first touch goes out within minutes.

(not to mention the increase in form responses we get from only needing ONE question!) 

AI isn't here to replace SDRs. Rob Cook and his team are living proof of that. It's just making the SDR job *more* human. You don't have to figure out who someone is anymore. You just have to figure out how to connect, and show up.  

IMO - inbound is one of (if not THE) most rewarding automation to start with in Clay from an ROI vs. effort perspective. 

You won't want to miss this one - link in the comments 👇🏽

content:
I've been recruiting for Clay's strategic finance team for over a year. We’re always searching, and after meeting hundreds of people, have only made 3 offers. We’re building something different.

Most finance teams I’ve come across fit in two buckets. At early-stage businesses, finance can research and strategize endlessly, but the reality is the outcome is binary and product-related. At late stage companies, you’re optimizing a machine that has already been built. For example, you might own pricing in one geography and product line. It’s important, tied to a lot of revenue, but relatively narrow.

Clay is at a unique moment where neither of those is true. The product works, the business is growing, and the problems are genuinely hard and wide open. So our team owns entire surfaces end-to-end in a way that almost never happens in finance. 

Zona is a good example. She took our pricing launch, spent a year on it across multiple iterations, worked with every corner of the company (product, sales, post-sales, marketing, etc.) and eventually launched something with a real impact on the business. She wasn’t a contributor - she was an owner. 

That’s not an exception. I intentionally want my team to feel extreme ownership and trust with our biggest initiatives, because it’s the only way to attract and retain truly exceptional people (it’s how I would choose a job!). I’m biased from my past hedge fund experience: I want to work with and learn from the best. The bar is high, and we don't hire often - but we’re looking for curious, highly motivated and fun-to-be-around teammates who can both think and execute on extremely wide and deep levels. 

We've hired operators and investors alike, and are solving for the right fit, not a typical resume. If what we’re building resonates with you, I’d love to chat.
We're specifically hiring for:

-Strategic Finance: own the biggest strategic bets at Clay
-FP&A: own how the business is performing and operationalizing the model into outcomes

We're also hiring in Data Analytics, Partnerships, and Accounting. Apply at the link in the comments.

I recently celebrated 3 years at Clay. 

It's been a wild journey – and I'm getting a rare moment of stillness and calm this Friday to reflect. 

The growth. The chaos. The learning. The people.

Three years ago I could NOT have imagined being where I am today — and I mean that in every way you could imagine. The things I've gotten to build, the lessons I've had to learn the hard way, and the humans who made all of it possible.

---

2 reasons I decided to join Clay all those years ago: 

1. I thought it would be really fun to work with Varun Anand on something real (we tried to write a newsletter together and that wasn't it)

2. Everyone I talked to was brilliant, inspirational, fun, and kind.

Three years later and 350+ people later – it's shocking to me how true #2 still is.

(#1 was also true but also it can sometimes be hard to work with your friends when you don't do a good job ... a story for another time). 

It is genuinely insane how much I learn everyday from the crazy problems we get to work on, the amazing things we get to create, but *more than anything else* – the new colleagues who continue to teach me brilliant new things every day. 

Last night I got real sappy and gave a *bunch* of kudos to a bunch of colleagues (and not enough of them tbh), but on this Friday morning I want to give a public shout to someone who has had an unmistakably huge impact on my life and my ability to do my job well. 

🎉Rachel Hepworth 🎉

One of the most vulnerable things I can admit in public ... while I love what I get to do every day at Clay, from the team, to the product, to the things we get to build — I'm also flying half to fully blind 99% of the time.  

Because we're at the stage of growth and company where I'm doing a lot of this for the first time ever. 

Most of it actually. 

I don't know what I don't know about how to build and grow and lead a team in the way that this moment (and pretty much all future moments) demands.

And that's where Rachel has been extraordinary.

From day one, what stood out to me about Rachel is that she doesn't just have an incredible depth of experience (though she certainly has that as well). 

She's also razor-sharp. 

One of those people whom you can tell just *gets it*. 

But what makes her one-of-a-kind? She can take a problem I'm wrestling with in real time, filter it through her own lens and experience, AND come back with advice that is custom-tailored to the specific team, system, and situation I'm facing, with nuance to my personal context. 

I've had enough mentors to realize how rare that is. 

Many mentors who have "done it before" are quick to tell me the "right" way to do things. Rachel is great at recommending what she *thinks* is right (and she's often right 😅) , while ALSO adjusting to my context and providing incredible nuance and understanding. 

I wouldn't be half the leader — or the person — I am today without her guidance and wisdom.

Thank you Rachel  🙏🏽

content:
When Varun Anand asked me if I wanted to start Clay's education function I said ... Absolutely not 😅

Because most "education" is really just a dressed up version of the military-industrial factory complex. 

Have you ever asked yourself, "𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘪𝘴 𝘴𝘤𝘩𝘰𝘰𝘭 𝘧𝘰𝘳"? 

It's definitely not for learning. 

School is for compliance. Obedience. Performance based on standards. 

Most SaaS education is the same. 

Click this button. Follow this workflow. Get this certification. 

"Education" encourages people to 𝘤𝘰𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘵 dots. 

𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 is all about 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘯𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 dots. 

Learning is about rewiring how you think. Embracing different perspectives. Acquiring skills that change your mindset. 

Learning is transformational. 
Education is transactional. 

Lucky for me - Varun was totally aligned.

So we built Clay University - because you 𝘥𝘰 need the content foundation. 

But we've 𝘢𝘭𝘴𝘰 built cohorts and workshops for experiential learning. 
We've created certifications based on 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘦𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘺 (not a multiple choice quiz). 
We're building an entire talent marketplace (and training program). 
We're hosting Clay Cup, the world's biggest GTME competition. 
We have 94+ Clay Clubs around the world. 
And we're growing our 30,000+ Slack Community everyday. 

And we're still just getting started. 

"Education" (read: learning) is rapidly becoming critical for AI-era software companies. 

Because the "Click-and-follow" era of SaaS is over. 

Keeping up with the latest tools requires constant evolutions in mindset and problem-solving.

The companies that create ecosystems that fuel transformative learning will create communities unlike anything we've seen. 

Call that "Learning Led Growth"

At HubSpot, Founding CEO Brian Halligan once told me in a meeting: "We don't really do good with feelings. Let's get to the numbers."
 
Co-founder, Dharmesh Shah used to say it more bluntly: "In God we trust. All others bring data."
 
That's the culture I came up in.
 
I recorded a Move the Needle podcast episode with Yash Tekriwal 🤔 this week. (Link: https://lnkd.in/ej9dMvnt.) He runs ecosystem at Clay. (An AI-driven sales and marketing automation platform.) We're customers and I expected Clay might run like HubSpot did: in a very data-driven way.
 
As I was interviewing Yash, I realized a lot of what he does at Clay can't be attributed directly to revenue.
 
So, I asked him how Clay decides what to invest in for things they can't easily attribute: their NYC Subway ad campaign, the in-person workshops they run with prospects and customers, the 84 Clay Club chapters around the world.
 
He told me Clay tracks two types of data.
 
"One is what everyone is used to. It's the financial metrics, the tracking, the planning, the spreadsheet."
 
"And then the other is just the feeling. Are you feeling the pull of the market? Are you feeling the pull of customers?"
 
Watch the clip below.
 
This mirrors a conversation I keep having with my team. We obsess over leading and lagging indicators, as we should. But when launching a new product with a new value prop (like our AI analyst and MCP server: https://databox.com/ai), the first clue it's working is in customer conversations and early adoption, not in sales and financial impact yet.
 
To get these capabilities into the hands of builders, I've been hands-on building a new partner program (https://lnkd.in/enXXktgh) at Databox. People like Rick Kranz, László Fazakas, Max Traylor, Paul Sullivan, Kamil Rextin Claudio Lira, PhD and a bunch of others are building unique products on top of our MCP server, leveraging our new AI Analyst.
 
We've acquired a handful of new customers so far. Our funnel is building (as is theirs). That's the hard data. 
 
But the bigger reason I'm all in is the feedback I'm getting from these builders. They're building products around our business, willingly open-sourcing them, and proactively marketing both their work and our platform.
 
Rick Kranz published something that said, "The Databox MCP is one of the most significant AI related tools released this year. It gives us access to all our structured data from many diverse complex sources in one reliable pipeline. This allows AI to perform feats of analysis that were impossible before."
 
Unprompted quotes like these make me confident the sales volume will follow.
 
Halligan had another thing he used to say to managers: "Are you in the coal face?" Meaning: are you working alongside your front-line team, talking to prospects, partners, and customers?
 
I am. Yash is. Are you? Do you feel it?

content:
I'm here today to give brett weinberg (why can’t I tag you!) a public shoutout for using AI the *right* way.  

He didn't asking AI to write something for him with 0 thought. 
He wasn't trying to take a shortcut. 
He wasn't even looking for answers.

He was *thinking* with it.

Brett had a hunch — that teaching Clay should be built around backwards design. Start with the outcome, work backwards to the inputs. He brought that raw idea to Claude and used it as a sparring partner to pressure-test, expand, and sharpen the concept.

By the end of the conversation, he had a full curriculum framework, with a custom excalidraw flowchart to boot.

And that's what I think most people get wrong about AI right now.
The dominant narrative is: give AI a task, get a result, save time.

So it's no shock when people wring their hands in the air and say "AI isn't good enough yet". 

But, IMO, the real unlock with AI *isn't* automation. 

It's *augmentation*.

Brett wasn't saving time. He was investing it. He went back and forth, pushed on ideas, asked Claude to build on what they'd developed together. AI didn't replace his thinking — it accelerated it.

He moved beyond prompting, into collaborating. 

Most people I see are using AI like a vending machine — put in a prompt, get out a deliverable.

Learn to think with AI. Not just through it.

content:
Account Agents are now live in Clay! To show you how it works, we’re taking you to one of the last old chess parlors in Greenwich Village. 

If you're in sales or marketing, what you already know about an account should decide how you respond to it. A demo request from a company that trialed you last quarter shouldn't be handled like one from a company that's never heard of you. One goes straight to the AE who knows what stalled. The other starts at qualification.

The problem is you write automation rules before you know which accounts will hit them. The account's real history sits in your CRM and Gong calls until a rep digs it out.

Account Agents put that history inside the play. Drop one into any workflow as a node and it arrives knowing every touch, call, deal, and past conclusion on the account. You draw the possible paths when you build the play. When a trigger fires, the agent picks which action to take and the Workflow runs it. What the agent learns gets saved back to Audiences, so your plays get smarter with every run. 

Account Agents in Workflows are in open beta for Enterprise, Growth, and Launch customers.

When we first invented the GTM Engineer title 3 years ago – it just felt like a more pointed variation of what I'd been doing for years - low-code automation.

I was skeptical. Varun Anand was incredibly optimistic (as always). 

And what I've learned since ... being pointed matters. 

In every facet of life. 

In community and friendship, if you're "liked" by everyone, you're loved by no one (harsh but true).  

The same is true in work. 

I used to be incredibly bullish on "low-code automation" as the future of ops. It's why I built an agency in the space doing the work. 

But the reality is that you need to focus on ~simple~ problems first - and ones that extend naturally from there. 

Turns out, GTM was the perfect blend of a wide enough playground with enough specificity in the AI native era that it made a massive splash in the market. 

The role is ever evolving, as model capabilities and tooling gets 10x seemingly ever month. 

I think I talk to at least 3 people everyday who feel like it's impossible to keep up. 

If we're being honest - it totally is. 

Instead, solve your problems from first principles. You don't *need* to keep up with everything happening in industry. You just need to keep up with the 20% of things that will create the 80% of outcomes for you in your work. 

Still kind of crazy to think about how this movement has taken off - excited to be continuing to build at the forefront of it with this community ❤️

content:
Order matters.

One of the biggest mistakes I see GTMEs make:
jumping *straight* to the most ambitious automation—AI-generated outbound, full account mapping, enterprise-wide relationship orchestration.

That's like trying to build the penthouse before you've poured the foundation.

There's a specific sequence to building AI-powered relationship infrastructure.

If you skip steps, the whole thing collapses. 

But if you follow the order, each layer makes the next one dramatically easier.

---
Level 1: Enable Your Team with Better Data

Start here. Before you automate anything, equip the people you already work with the data they need to build better relationships. 

• Give your AEs the enrichment they need. 
• Surface the context that makes conversations meaningful. 
• Make sure everyone has the intelligence to be great at their jobs.

--- 
Level 2: Generate First Touchpoints

Once your team is operating with better data, then you can start helping them *initiate* relationships. 

• Go from research automation ➡️ draft the first message
• Interact with people engaging on socials 
• *Don't* over-automate. You're not replacing the relationship—you're lowering the friction to start it.

---
Level 3: Scale Across Enterprise Orgs

Now you can think bigger. How do you help your team build relationships across entire buying committees? How do you map influence across a 50,000-person company? How do you ensure every stakeholder has a path to engage with you?

Order isn't sexy, but it's mission critical. The biggest mistake you can make is biting off more than you chew to start. 

This is going to be a key part of weeks 1 and 2 in the new GTME course we're launching next week!

content:
"Education" is having a resurgence because of AI.

Product quality is only half the battle. The other half is the skills gap.

And the fear gap.

“If you build an airplane and people are afraid of anything that flies, you can’t just say there’s something wrong with the people.” - Richard Hendricks, Silicon Valley

AI isn't another a button-clicking enablement to teach your team. Effective AI training is about changing *how people think*. 

But, hot take, most companies are doing it wrong.

Because "education" has a marketing problem.

When we hear education, we think of systems built for the industrial age.

Textbooks. Lectures. Standardized tests.

Tools designed to cultivate compliance and teach obedience.

Not creativity.
Not individuality.
Not critical thinking.

*Those* skills are the results of *learning*.

When we work on novel problems we care about, with people we care about, we create learning moments that don’t happen in command-and-control classrooms.

Real projects.
Thoughtful feedback.
Intentional reflection.

These are the pillars of learning.

Learning happens in community. Through experiences. Through failure.

Videos are necessary, but not sufficient for transformation.

They work for early adopters because early adopters are trained learners. They create their own communities, projects, and feedback loops around the content.

But lifelong learners are maybe 10% of the people you need to reach.

What about the other 90%?

To reach them at scale, you need community, programs, and experiences.

That’s not education.

It’s ecosystem building.

Traditionally, "Education" is hired as a check-the-box function. So teams create content and certifications for customers to also check the box.

But what if, instead of checking boxes, we built bridges?

What if we built a *whole team* of the absolute best people in learning, community, and program design?

That’s the question we’re answering at Clay.

We’ve built the early hubs and spokes of our GTME ecosystem:

Community
Startup programs
Campus programs
Online cohorts
IRL workshops
University content
Certifications and badges
Partnerships and programs
Talent matching

We're hiring rapidly to expand the scale and quality of our growing ecosystem.

content:
Everyone is still prompting AI like they're searching Google. 
One vague sentence and hoping for magic.

The fix is stupidly simple. Stop making demands. Start asking strategic questions.

You'll see a 10x increase in your output quality.

Think about it. When you hand a task to a brand new intern who is eager to please but has zero context on your business — you wouldn't say "write me a personalized first line for this prospect."

You'd walk them through your thinking and process. You'd help them understand what good looks like.

That's Socratic prompting. Here's an example of a *horrible* (but very common) AI outbound copywriting prompt I see at Clay all the time: 

"𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗹 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 {𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹𝗡𝗮𝗺𝗲} 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗼𝘄: {𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵}."

Generic prompt ➡️ generic output 🤷‍♂️ 

✅ a better way: 
"𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗯𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽: 
𝟭) 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 {𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹𝗡𝗮𝗺𝗲}'𝘀 𝗿𝗼𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 {𝗧𝗶𝘁𝗹𝗲} 𝗮𝘁 {𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆}. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗱𝗮𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗮𝘆?

content:
Izzy Kim and I have been neck-deep in resumes for the past couple weeks for the Cohorts role at Clay.

The response has been *incredible*. Truly!

But I feel like it's my public duty to say something that might save a few people some heartache:

In the era of AI, there is no excuse for a bad resume.

A few things I'm seeing way too often:

1. Resumes longer than one page.
Unless you *literally* saved the world, your resume should be one page. If you must have a second page, it better be extraordinarily interesting — not an overflow of bullet points that didn't fit on page one.

2. Bullet points that are multiple sentences long.
If a bullet point needs two or three sentences to land, it's not a bullet point — it's a paragraph pretending to be one. Keep them tight. One to three exceptions max across the entire resume.

3. No quantification. No impact.
Every bullet should answer: so what? If you can attach a number, a percentage, a result — do it. If you can't quantify it, at least illustrate the impact. "Managed social media" tells me nothing. "Grew Instagram from 2K to 18K in 6 months" tells me far more.

4. Too many bullets per experience.
Three to four per role. That's it. If you have eight bullets under one job, it tells me you don't know what you're most proud of. Also, high skimmability is of the utmost importance. Again, know the game you're playing. 

Just put yourself in a recruiter's shoes.

They have hundreds to *thousands* of resumes to screen. In addition to schedule calls. In addition to finding new candidates. And dealing with a million other things. 

Which means .... they're spending 30 to 60 seconds on your resume before deciding - "is this person worth talking to?" The only question in their head is: "Does this person have the background and skills I need for this role?"

Every formatting decision you make should make that question easier to answer — NOT harder.

If your resume is adding friction to that 60-second scan, you are actively decreasing your chances of making it to an interview. 

To top it all off - an intelligent conversation with AI can help you fix all of this in 20 minutes. 

"Help me make this line more concise, give me 5 variations for the rewrite"

"I want to quantify the impact of my time in X job better. Here's what I did ..." 

"Okay – now pretend you're a recruiter for Y role at Z company. What are all the holes you'd poke in my resume – or reasons you *wouldn't* advance me to the next stage? Analyze each section of my resume step-by-step and think of reasons at each stage. Try to come up with at least 5, but if you can't come up with any genuine ones - don't make any up!" 

I don't care *what* you're applying for – designer, PM, marketer, salesperson – not having the initiative to think through the above implicitly tells people you're not high agency.

And maybe one of the *only* skills that remains relevant in the era of AI is high agency. 

P.S - h/t George Mack on this https://lnkd.in/ghtRtAUK

Interviewing for a new role has not evolved for 2025/6, so we're trying something new.

The old way: 
1️⃣ Apply for a job online, and likely get connected to the hiring manager through a warm intro.
2️⃣ Recruiter screen.
3️⃣ Hiring manager screen.
4️⃣ Then another round... (and maybe another).
5️⃣ If you make it, do a take home.
6️⃣ Invite for final round, where you likely put in hours of prep. Then come onsite for several hours.
7️⃣ If all goes well, coordinate references.

After weeks and hours of your life, you find out if you get the job or not.

The reality is the best candidates just are not going to put the time in for this. They are too busy being top performers in their current roles.

Over the next 2 weeks we are going to attempt to shrink down the above multi-week (month?) process into one day, where we are hand picking top 1% talent to participate in an Enterprise Growth Strategist hiring day.

How it will work:
1️⃣ Quick recruiter chat to walk you through the role, team and logistics of the day to see if you want to commit the time.

3️⃣ Come onsite in our NYC or SF office, meet the team and other EGS. Do a mock kickoff workshop with us and a deep dive on your career background + aspirations. This will take ~3 hours.

First, it was iPads
Then, Chromebooks
Now, AI

Each was going to revolutionize education

Each helped a tech giant train the next gen how to use their tools with ultimately little to negative educational payoff

Here's what ACTUALLY seems to happen as quoted by this neuroscientist

"Gen Z is the first generation in modern history to underperform us on basically every cognitive measure we have, from basic attention to memory, to literacy, to numeracy, to executive functioning, to EVEN GENERAL IQ, even though they go to more school than we did."

"Once countries adopt digital technology widely in schools, performance goes down significantly, to the point where kids who use computers about five hours per day in school for learning purposes will score over two-thirds of a standard deviation LESS than kids who rarely or never touch tech at school. And that’s across 80 countries.”

I do think there are other social factors at play, but I haven't seen any real evidence that sitting in front of a screen, big or small, is good for young people (or anyone)

Here's how we're thinking about technology use at Forge Prep

This is taken directly from some docs sent to parents at enrollment

Phones Don't Belong Here

Campus is mobile-free. Students don't bring phones to school, i.e, not in lockers, not in backpacks, nowhere. Every minute matters so we don’t want Guides spending time policing devices.

This isn't negotiable, and it's also not a sacrifice. Evidence shows students prefer it and early data suggests this is better for student achievement and engagement.

Technology Serves Creation, Not Consumption

Students use technology constantly at Forge to build, design, research, code, film, and document their work. Computers, cameras, design software, and even smartphones are used when projects require them. (Note: we will provide the smartphones)

What we don't allow: technology that displaces thinking, fragments attention, or trains passive consumption habits. YouTube tutorials to learn a skill? Yes. YouTube rabbit holes? No.

The goal isn't less technology. It's better technology habits which encourage using tools to create rather than consume.

content:
Retention isn’t luck. It’s built in onboarding. Time kills deals, but *also* kills activation.

Here’s what we learned talking with Lauren Humphrey, who built customer success at Brightwheel and Gusto (and now runs Mintable).

Most teams obsess over closing deals. But if you don’t get customers activated-fast-you’re burning CAC and momentum.

Brightwheel saw this firsthand. Deals were flowing in, but a huge chunk of new users never made it through activation.

No one knew why.

No one owned the timeline.

Lauren’s playbook:

• Treat onboarding as the extension of sales. The same energy, the same discipline.
• Use time as your forcing function. Pick a number (Brightwheel chose 30 days). Break onboarding into weekly milestones. Track it like pipeline.
• Earn the right to automate. Start manual. Sit with reps. Whiteboard every step. That’s where the friction lives.
• Build structure and urgency. Deadlines turn onboarding from an endless project into a measurable process.
• Find leverage through alignment. Sales sets the promise, onboarding fulfills it, product reinforces it.

Brightwheel ran small experiments. Group onboarding worked (social learning is real). “Hot pass” didn’t (customers weren’t ready). They documented *everything* so the team spoke the same language.

As we scaled, efficiency mattered. No one wants a long onboarding. Customers value speed. Brightwheel switched calls to texts and users *loved* it, plus reps saved hours.

Most people wanted to be firefighters, astronomers, or doctors when they were asked what they wanted to be when they grow up.

Not me. 

I wanted to be super, super effective at using B2B SaaS.

Okay, fine, I actually wanted to be an architect (RIP). 

But digital productivity unexpectedly became a huge passion of mine when I started spending 40 (60?)+ hours a week on a computer. 

I remember the first time I saw how much more effectively bankers used Excel when they were operating *everything* from their keyboards.

I thought, "Shouldn't I ... use my whole computer that way?"

content:
If you care too much about how you look, you will never master anything worthwhile.

This gets harder and harder as we get more senior in our careers and lives.

A lot of our self-confidence and reputations *comes* from looking smart, capable, and impressive.

It's the “I’m the Head of Data, so I can’t look like I don’t know what I’m doing” trap.
The “I’m our VP of Sales, so asking dumb questions is off limits” trap.

But every single time you learn something important, you have to look absolutely clueless first.

You have to ask the “obvious” questions.
You have to fumble with tools in front of people who already knew how to use them.
You have to admit, “I have no idea what I’m doing here.”

If you’re always focused on how you look, you remove the spaciousness needed for true learning to emerge.

You start performing instead of practicing.
You start hiding mistakes instead of embracing them.
You start caring about applause instead of progress.

And that’s the death of growth.

If you want to get good at anything, you have to get comfortable trying, failing, looking silly, and smashing repeat.

Yesterday, we ran the FIRST EVER MCP hackathon we've done with OpenAI in London. 

30+ builders. 
One room. 
Pure chaos (the good kind).

People built things we didn't expect. One team created a full database for podcast mining and research. Another built an AI-powered GTM war room — a single command center where sellers get everything they need to work deals, turbocharged by AI.

It was early. Baby steps, if anything. But the level of enthusiasm and creativity the builders brought to the room was such validating proof of *why* we're going all in on Europe today with the launch of our London office.

But it reinforced something else I keep coming back to - *especially* in the era of AI, most human wins.

The barrier between technical skill and creativity has collapsed. *Everyone* at the hackathon was using AI to build tools and workflows they never could have before— coding with Codex, leveraging Claygent in Clay. 

But it wasn't perfect. 

We watched people spend 30 minutes trying to get a simple HTTP API call working. We saw folks reaching for MCP calls when a straightforward API call would've done the job. 

You cannot let AI substitute your ability to think critically through problems, or learn what you need to, when you need to. 

People were afraid of the terminal. *Don't be*. 

Learn technical concepts so that you *know* what's happening behind the scenes with AI. 

Deeply understand the difference between APIs and MCPs. Know when you should reach for one vs. the either. 

Dissect a basic HTTP/API call. Dig deep. *Acquire the skill*, and THEN augment it with AI. 

People are in such a rush to build that they're skipping over the skill acquisition piece - which is actually the most valuable part. 

The next decade will keep leveling the playing field between "technical" and "non-technical" people. It's never been a better time to be a builder.

Which means it's never been a more important time to become a technically savvy builder — someone who understands the fundamentals, not just the tools.

European GTM teams face a harder version of the same problems — fragmented data across markets, lower coverage rates, country-by-country buying playbooks.

What is unequivocally true is that computational thinking is coming for all GTM jobs.

That does *not* mean that you have to know how to code. 

It *does* mean that you have to understanding how computers "think". 

And what history has shown us time and time again is that when the discipline of engineering gets infused with traditionally *non-engineered* industries - there's a step change in productivity and output. 

Think about it: 

• Engineering + Finance ➡️ Quantitative Trading 
• Engineering + Manufacturing ➡️ Industrial Revolution 
• Engineering + Restaurants ➡️ Fast Food Revolution

This trend is now unmistakably coming for GTM. 

What has traditionally kept GTM so resilient from engineering innovation is the highly subjective and human oriented nature of the work. We haven't historically had computational ways of processing calls, or messages, or generating creative copy. 

GenerativeAI has fundamentally changed this. For the first time in history, it's actually possible to scale subjective outputs. 

But you need to embrace systems and computational thinking to become a part of this revolution. For example, you need to: 

→ Understand lists vs. objects

content:
My career took off the day I admitted something I'd been hiding for years:

I'm not that smart.

Let me explain.

I spent most of my high school and college career *masquerading* as a smart person.

Perfect SAT score. Above average grades. 60+ AP credits. 

But I didn't achieve those things because I was intelligent. I acquired those accolades because I was good at the *game of modern education*. 

Memorize, regurgitate onto a test, move on.

I was *collecting* dots without taking the time to properly *connect* them. 

I don't remember most of what I "learned" in high school or college. Which is a *shame* because I had the privilege of being in some *amazing* classrooms with world-class teachers.

BUT, when I finally graduated – I was free to follow my own curiosity. 

I dove into low-code tools — Zapier, Airtable, PhantomBuster. I took Seth Godin's altMBA. I started building things. 

And ... I realized that I was slower than most people at digesting new concepts. I *really* need to understand something from the absolute fundamental principles to have any chance of retaining it.

Duh.

I was just always afraid of ... asking dumb questions. Because I cared more about how my own intelligence was *perceived*, rather than the quality of my intelligence itself. 

Fast forward almost a decade later and we've come full circle. Today, I *do* deeply understand the worlds I live in *and* I am an incredibly quick study. 

But not because I'm "gifted". Because I worked hard to build a true foundation of knowledge so strong that adding new concepts are just little building blocks on top of an incredibly stable structure (instead of a house of cards). 

But my ultimate lesson is that I couldn't tap into my strengths until I was willing to admit my weaknesses.

content:
IKEA didn’t start with disrupting furniture. It started as a delivery service (for almost everything - from pens to wallets to groceries)

Clay didn't start in GTM. It started as a horizontal automation tool.

This pattern is impossible to ignore – many generational companies start out with much broader, less specialized ambitions.

Samsung started as a general trading company.
Slack was (yet another) attempt to create the world's best video game.
Corning was a glass producer.

We love the “big vision” founder story. The "Steve jobs" archetypes who "see" the future and bend reality to their will.

But that narrative is more often hindsight bias than it is truth.

IKEA’s founder? Started with what he had. Sold whatever people needed. Over time, they saw patterns in needs for furniture. There was no master plan - just a series of small, practical moves that were constant adaptations to what they were learning.

When I was in school at UVA, I learned a term for this counter-causal style of entrepreneurial decision-making: effectuation.

Effectuation is a framework of thinking that focuses on starting with your *available* resources (who you are, what you know, and whom you know) to create new opportunities, instead of setting a goal and working backwards from it.

And what I've learned over the years is that these principles aren't *just* what the most effective founders utilize to navigate uncertain greenfield terrain.

They're also the principles that the best startup *teams* embody to make decisions quickly, adapt to dynamic environments, and make lemonade. 

The 5 core principles to effectuation: 

🐦 1. Bird in Hand: Use what you’ve got. Your skills, your network, your weird collection of Google Sheets. Build from there. No magic required.
📉 2. Affordable Loss: Don’t bet the farm. Bet what you can lose and keep rolling. I’ve lost count of how many mini-experiments I’ve run that never saw daylight (and that’s fine).
🎨 3. Crazy Quilt: Bring in partners, early users, the random guy in Slack with strong opinions. Co-create. Patchwork is a feature, not a bug.
🍋 4. Lemonade: Surprise! The thing you planned isn’t what people want. Great-pivot. Make the new thing. Sell lemonade if life hands you lemons (or, you know, if orange juice tanks).
✈️ 5. Pilot in the Plane: You’re not a passenger. You’re flying the damn thing. You shape the market as you go.

Every standout startup employee I know operates this way. Not just the founders.

(And if you’re thinking “I don’t have the founder gene”- good news, nobody does, it doesn't exist)

It's a mindset and a skillset you can hone and cultivate 💥

content:
Most AI projects fail because teams try to sprint before they can crawl.

Huge budgets, big promises, shiny decks with “transformation” in bold font.

But I've seen a dark pattern show up over and over again with orgs trying to implement AI:

• Teams try to automate everything on day one.
• The first rollout hits a wall (surprise: edge cases).
• People get frustrated when the results are… not magical.
• Someone says “AI is garbage.”
• Project quietly dies.

AI is not a magic button.
It’s more like onboarding a new employee who doesn’t speak your language (yet).

If you fired every new hire that didn't crush their job on day 1, you'd have a total headcount of 0.

Here's how we crawl, walk, run with new AI use cases internally at Clay: 

• Start small. Pick ONE use case.
• Test with a tiny group.
• Get feedback (the good, the bad, the “wait, why did it do THAT?”).
• Iterate.
• THEN expand to a few more people. Ideally core-stakeholders with high propensity to give you valuable feedback.
• Repeat.
• Only after things are humming, roll out org-wide.

AI needs training.
Systems need tuning. 
Change is a process, not a performance.

If you’re feeling stuck, or your team is on the “AI is garbage” train, *slowing down* might be the counterintuitive answer in a world that seems to be moving faster and faster.

Remember that slow is smooth and smooth is fast.

content:
90% of my AI posts are about automation & efficiency.

But I recommend AI *personally* all the time for not automation reasons 👀

You can (and IMO, *should*) use AI to augment *meaning*, not just output.

Here's a crazy statistic: 2.9% of all Claude chats are *affective* in nature, meaning that they're emotional or feelings-based in nature 👀

Using AI to level up your emotional intelligence, support, and problem-solving is actually 10x more powerful than using it to automate mundane work.

My one caveat – be *careful* in how you prompt AI to give you advice, or provide support.

Remember that AI is *designed* to support you and be helpful to you ... even if you don't deserve it.

That sounds harsh, but if you went to your best friends for advice on how you handled a situation, you *don't* want them to lie to you or sugarcoat it. You want the truth.

(and if you don't want the truth that's okay, maybe you do just need support – but remember that long-term only the truth will set you free).

For example, there's a big difference in taking screenshots of a charged text conversation with a friend and the following two prompts:

1. "Is this person being combative and immature in this conversation?"

2. "Analyze the following conversation between two individuals and create an assessment of the maturity + conflict levels of both sides, and opportunities for improvement for both parties, if any" 

I used the second prompt recently on a combative text exchange I had with a friend. And while I felt supported in feeling that I was on the receiving end of some immature communication, I *also* got some pretty good advice on when I was also responding in childish ways that weren't helping the situation. 

Remember to always create the space & opportunity for neutral analysis, and I promise you'll see incredible changes in both your personal and professional life 
❤️

content:
Yesterday I was consoling a friend going through a tough time. She asked how I always stay "calm", and I said: "because I know what rock bottom looks like". 

Story time 👇🏽

In January of 2015, I woke up in a hospital bed after a car accident. My face was shattered. I underwent an 8-hour surgery to reconstruct my face, and missed the spring semester of my first year in college. 

After months of hard recovery, my reaction was ... to double down on the Type A person that I was. 

I became a machine. 

Summer classes. 
Full-on grind mode. 
Overloading credits every semester. 

But I left my feelings behind.

When graduation rolled around the corner, I realized that I had made up for lost time – but the stuff that I remembered? 

It wasn't my grades, my internships, or my trophies. 

It was the late-night conversations around the firepit. 
Poker Tuesdays. 
Dancing on tables.
Falling asleep in a pile of leaves.
Crying on a friend’s shoulder.
Laughing until you can’t breathe.

AI is cool. Automation is cool. And I will continue to nerd out with you all constantly on both. 

But after spending my first weekend in a long time not touching my laptop, I'm re-learning the lesson 21-year Yash felt viscerally at graduation.  

Invest in your skills and success, but not at the expense of your life and health.

I haven't done the best job of this in 2025. 

And to be fair - it is easier said than done in the startup world. Particularly in the hyper-growth phase Clay is in, and *especially* when you enjoy your work as much as I do (which is an incredible privilege). But it's worth the constant balancing act. 

Maybe this isn't really the right content for LinkedIn ... but it's what came off the keyboard this morning, so 🤷🏽‍♂️. 

tl;dr - it's summer, enjoy your life, remember to go touch some grass because life can be shorter than you ever imagined 🌳

P.S - For anyone curious - full story on the aforementioned accident linked in the comments👇🏽

"That's a brilliant idea – but it won't scale" 😭

My sales manager crushed my soul with those 6 words in 2019.

I'd been experimenting with post-call emails: Instead of the boring "next steps + agenda" template, I added relevant TED talks or articles based on our conversation. With a personal quote that connected to what we'd discussed.

It was working. 30-40% higher engagement on qualified deals. 

I was giddy. 

But his critique was fair. 

This only worked for *me*, because I was a voracious consumer of knowledge. Training other team members to do this would add hours of time that *still* weren't justified by the results. 

—

Fast forward to 2025: This DOES scale.

Finding relevant though leadership from a call transcript and including a relevant quote can now be fully automated with AI. 

The naysayers think we're heading for spam cannon hell. But here's what they're missing:

**Spam cannons don't work.**

Companies spraying generic AI slop will lose. Hard.

These companies might spam people for a brief period - but they'll stop after they go out of business. 

👉 The winners will combine *scale* with *thoughtfulness*.

Here's the two-step playbook:

1️⃣ **First step (necessary but not sufficient):**
Automate the data monkey work. URL copying. Whitespace deletion. Format standardization.
This is work humans *shouldn't* do anyway.

2️⃣ **Second step (where the magic happens):**
Use AI to amplify human connection at scale. Personalized insights. Thoughtful touchpoints. Creative engagement that actually resonates.

The constraint isn't manual effort anymore.

It's imagination.

P.S - What I love most about this tactic is that to *truly* make it work - you can't fully automate it. You need sales reps to also be consuming the content thoughtfully, and tying it back to the part that matters more than anything else – building the relationship.

content:
A shocking number of startup folks (even aspiring founders!) don't understand how to value equity. 

Let's dig in 👇🏽

Here’s one (over-simplified) way to ball-park it (none of this is financial advice).

Principles
• Earlier join = lower cash, higher equity. Risk ↔ reward.
• You’re trading guaranteed salary for a shot at an equity payday. If that’s not true where you’re interviewing, ask why.

Hypothetical offer:
Series A startup
• Cash: $100K salary
• Equity: 10K shares = 1% (valuation is $10M today, so face value ≈ $100K)

What *could* it be worth?
1️⃣ You think the business can 100× to $1B in ~5 years.

EDIT: Add your estimated probably of success in. Let's say you're bullish enough for it to be 20%,

2️⃣ Expect two more rounds: 15% dilution, then 10%.
• Ownership falls: 1% → 0.85% → 0.765%

3️⃣ Exit value: $1B × 0.765% x 20% ≈ $1.53M (risk-adjusted), $7.65M total. 

Compare to a big-co offer
• BigCo pays $300K cash. Over 5 years that’s $1.5M (ignoring raises/bonuses/taxes).

• If the startup hits, your total payoff there (cash + equity) is ~$8M. BigCo’s $1.5M is < 20% of that—despite triple the salary. However, the risk adjusted return is *about* equal, and big co is a safer bet in terms of what you *know* you'll put in the bank. 

Caveats
• Options vest over 4 years and have a strike price you’ll pay to exercise.
• Exit timing, taxes (ISO/NSO, AMT, long-term gains), and liquidation preferences all matter.
• Most startups don’t 100×—valuations can also go to zero.

All that said, there's also lots of intangibles to the (right) startup. Culture. Ownership. Learning. It goes on! 

Again, this is over simplified math just because many people I chat with don't know how to think about equitynkusr at this level. 

Again, to reiterate, not financial advice 😀

P.S - chat with o3 or Claude to help you think through *all* the details! 

P.P.S - these are all fictional numbers that make the math easy to do. The reality is that you offers will have more wonky/specific numbers in the real world. The point is not to benchmark off of these numbers - they're made up. Use benchmarking tools like Pave to think about if what you're getting is fair - then think about the math. 

👉 Questions, pushback, different heuristics? Drop them below!

One will flop.

You’re not hiring for polish. You’re hiring for hunger.

Anyone can explain product features. 
But the top 1%? They sound like advisors—not reps.
They help buyers understand their own problems better.
Even if the deal doesn’t close, the prospect walks away smarter.

Everyone thinks creativity is about having infinite options. Wrong. 

Constraints fuel breakthrough thinking, even in GTM. 

Consider Salesforce's early days. With no marketing budget, they created the "No Software" campaign - a constraint that forced them to pioneer SaaS messaging.

Or look at Warby Parker: shipping limitations led them to mail 5 frames for home trials, revolutionizing how we buy glasses.

The constraint-to-creativity pipeline in sales:

1. Scarcity → Focus
• Limited time with prospects? Craft tighter value props. 
• One study found sales pitches under 9 minutes had 2.5x higher close rates than 30-minute presentations

2. Boundaries → Innovation
• Can't get past gatekeepers? LinkedIn's Sales Navigator emerged from this exact constraint. 
• Today's best salespeople use pattern interrupts precisely because traditional methods are blocked.

3. Obstacles → Differentiation
• Everyone's inbox is flooded with emails? Leverage personalization to stand out.

content:
Steve Jobs famously called computers "bicycles for the mind."

People are treating AI like a car—hop in, turn off your brain, travel. 👎🏽

That's backwards.

AI should be an e-bike for the mind. Same rider, same journey, but with power assist when you hit the hills.

The difference matters. The MIT study making rounds (reduced to "ChatGPT makes you dumber") actually showed something *fascinating*. Participants who started with their own thinking, then added AI, showed higher brain activity than either approach alone.

I call this the "Tony Stark" principle 🤖

When Stark needs a new element in Iron Man 2, he doesn't say "Jarvis, create a new element." Instead:

• He guides Jarvis to digitize the expo map
• He directs the structural analysis
• He interprets the atomic patterns
• He discovers a new element

The AI augments his thinking—it doesn't replace it.

fwiw - This is why "AI SDRs" that promise to "do all your outbound" miss the mark. The best sales teams use AI differently: as intelligence amplifiers for signal detection, message iteration, and rapid experimentation. The human remains the strategist; AI accelerates the execution.

The bicycle didn't make human legs obsolete—it made them more powerful. The e-bike didn't eliminate pedaling—it made every push count for more.

That's your choice with AI: passenger or pilot?

Choose pilot. Your mind at the handlebars, AI in the assist. That's where the magic happens.

content:
Most job applications fail before you even start.

Because people don't understand the game that they're playing.

Job seekers, I cannot emphasize enough that companies are getting hundreds to *thousands* of applications for the same role.

And reaching out to a recruiter or someone at the company to "bump" your resume doesn't actually change your chances of *getting* an offer, just of getting a *response*.

Understand the game you are playing.

Good recruiters *want* to dig deep, find the hidden gems, see “the whole you”…

But when they're staring at 1,000+ resumes in a spreadsheet, they can't.

So they default to what’s easy to sort:

• Work experience
• School names
• Fancy job titles
• Keywords

(Take it from someone who’s been on both sides… it’s brutal.)

If your resume doesn’t scream “top candidate” in those first 10 seconds, it’s game over.

But you can still stand out *beyond* your resume: 

→ Make something unique that jumps out of the pile
→ Prove skills that don’t show up on paper
→ Show them you GET the company and can add value

Follow this framework, execute it perfectly, and you can even *create* jobs for yourself.

For example - we're not *currently* hiring for the education team at Clay.

*But*, if you were to:

• Attend Clay cohorts and draft a 💥 1-pager on what we should improve + how
• Film lessons/content of your own on topics you think we could cover better
• Think of all the reasons I might say "no" and address all of them in a FAQ doc ...

I would fight like hell to give you a chance, and I bet Varun Anand would be down to figure something out.

One of my biggest red flags – when someone tells me how much they *love* Clay, and then when I dig into *what* they love about Clay, I come to realize that they have *never* used the tool 🤦🏽‍♂️

Yes, the job market is competitive -But shockingly few people really go above and beyond – so opportunities await you if you're hungry enough. 

P.S - Extra effort ≠ high quality effort. 
I *have* seen videos of personal builds that people *think* are super impressive ... but they're just fine. 
Having a high bar for yourself and your taste matters too.

content:
My new favorite learning tip – use AI to put yourself in role of *teacher*, NOT student. 

Here's what I do: 

Create a Claude project called "[Subject] Teaching Assistant" and flip the script. Instead of asking Claude questions, you explain concepts TO Claude and let it play the confused student. If you're curious about the learning science behind this, it's called the "Feynman technique".

This transforms you from passive consumer of content to active teacher-learner.

Trying to explain complex concepts to a newbie is the *best* way to turn knowledge into wisdom. 

Last week, I used this to make sure *deeply* understood how LLMs work after watching some of Andrej Karpathy's brilliant YouTube videos.

In a world where AI is more and more capable of performing human level work – what inevitably remains your competitive advantage is curiosity, passion, and creativity. 

The setup is easy: 

1. Create a Claude project named "[Subject] Teaching Assistant"
2. Add this custom instruction (copy and adapt as needed):

"You are a curious but confused student learning about [subject]. [Optional - Insert specific resource, context, or link]. When I explain concepts, ask clarifying questions like a student would. Don't explain anything or make any assumptions for me, defer to asking questions. Point out gaps in my explanations, make incorrect "learnings" from explanations that could use improvements, request examples, and ask 'why' and 'how' questions. If my explanation is unclear or incorrect, get confused and ask for clarification. Help me identify what I don't fully understand by being an engaged, slightly skeptical student."

Then, start teaching. Even better, use voice mode to have a natural conversation with your eager AI student (or, Wispr flow). 

You might get frustrated early on when it misunderstands some of your initial explanations ... but *that's the point*. 

When you can explain it simply enough for a confused student to understand, you've truly mastered it.

Try it with something you're learning right now. You'll be surprised how quickly "playing teacher" exposes what you need to study next.

content:
99% of online education is content-focused.

But the best learning isn't rooted in content 👀

The first internet era was about *access*. MOOCs promised ivy league education for everyone, for free.

Mission accomplished. You can now take Harvard's entire CS curriculum online.

So why are completion rates stuck at 3-5%? 🥵

Because access ≠ learning.

If the internet era was about access, the AI era is about *application*.

Not "can I find the information?" but "can I actually do something with it?"

Think about the last skill that actually changed how you work. I'm betting it involved:

• 👩‍👩‍👧‍👧 Community (people who pushed you)  
• ⚒️ Experience (actually doing the thing)  
• 🚩 Failure (knowing what bad looks like so you can better learn what good looks like)

Don't get me wrong, content is necessary for great learning. It's just not sufficient. 

Content is just guardrails. Real learning happens when you struggle with hard problems alongside generous peers.

Doing beats watching. Every. Single. Time.

—

At Clay, we launched cohorts exactly one year ago. Everything is live, practical, and community-driven.

The ratio of content to work is 30/70, not the other way around. And it's been going incredibly well 🚀

When we designed cohorts, I was constantly thinking about the most impactful online learning experience I'd ever had – the altMBA. 

In altMBA, there was ~38 minutes *total* of recorded content from Seth over 4 weeks. And there was ~70-80 *hours* of live, interactive, thought-provoking collaborative work and discussion. 

That's a 1/99 ratio of content to experience 👀

Clay Cohorts are a bit different. We're teaching more technical skills, and we're doing it all for *free* (altMBA was $5K tuition, and had a 1:10 student to coach ratio). 

But we have some big things planned for the end of the year. Expanding beyond Clay 101, offering smaller, more focused, but longer live learning experiences, and rethinking the entire learning journey for students in an AI-first world. 

I'm incredibly excited - stay tuned for more.

It’s not the features or price. It’s whether you’re working with vendors or partners.

The Attention team proved this perfectly.

Facilitating one-on-one coaching sessions, hands-on workshops, strategic brainstorming for future use cases. They treated our success as theirs.

Vendors measure contract value. Partners measure your outcomes.

Stop buying software. Start investing in partnerships.

content:
Whether or not you realize it, you chase alpha everyday. 

• Betting on the shortest line at the grocery store 
• Trying new AI tools that promise to 10x your output
• Training those new tactics against that {insert sport} rival you want to beat

In finance, "alpha" represents outperformance over market benchmarks. In other words - your competitive edge.

In everyday life, you chase alpha to save time, to increase productivity, or to find an edge over your competitors. 

In GTM, it's what separates market-beating teams from everyone else.

We've studied the patterns across top-performing GTM teams at companies like Anthropic, Vanta, and Canva, and they all share three key traits:

1️⃣ They find unique data advantages others miss
• Certemy identifies companies with compliance problems by tracking OSHA violations
• Intercom analyzes the breadth of support documentation to find perfect-fit targets
• Rutter spots high-value executives needing financial products the moment conference attendee lists go public Google Doc

2️⃣ They run experimental high-alpha plays
• Verkada generates thousands of personalized landing pages with company logos and specifics
• Rippling uses Google Maps to find corporate addresses and calculates commuting distances for precision direct mail
• Vanta builds personalized business reviews using product usage patterns

3️⃣ They build GTM engineering cultures
The outdated model where SDRs prospect, AEs close, and RevOps manage systems separately is being replaced by integrated teams that can find, test, and scale approaches faster.
At Anthropic, their Sales Ops team automates lead enrichment and routing so salespeople focus exclusively on high-value conversations.

—

The brutal reality: there is no permanent competitive advantage in GTM, only the continuous pursuit of temporary ones.

At first, the continuous chase of GTM alpha might sounds like a sisyphean hamster wheel of doom that ends in a weird malthusian dystopia. 

But at it's heart - it's continuous learning. Agility. The ability to adapt with the times and reinvent your offering as the world changes. 

The winners of modern GTM aren't following time-old playbooks—they're writing new ones every quarter.

Companies building AI-forward GTM engineering organizations will find alpha—others will get left behind.

content:
Learning is a journey through incompetence. And that's the point.

We've been taught that education is about accumulating knowledge, checking boxes, and avoiding mistakes.

Wrong.

Real learning happens when we struggle through our own incompetence - that uncomfortable space where we know enough to see our flaws but haven't mastered them yet.

Think about it:
• You don't learn to cook by memorizing recipes, you learn by cooking 
• You don't learn to code by reading documentation, you learn by coding
• You don't learn leadership from a textbook, you learn by leading 

You learn by doing. By failing. By trying again.

This is the biggest problem with the modern "standard" for online learning - it's content-driven. 

Online videos and guides are necessary, but not sufficient for true learning. 

You need experiential learning too: 
• You don't learn prompt engineering from watching videos, you learn by using ChatGPT
• You don't learn notion from templates, you learn by building in Notion
• You don't learn gtm engineering from a blog post, you learn by working in Clay (#cohorts!) 

The best teachers understand this. Their job isn't to lecture - it's to create spaces where students can safely explore their weaknesses.

That's why we built cohorts at Clay - and, in my opinion, why we've been overwhelmed with the demand. 

People *want* to learn new tools and skills. They just want better ways to learn than a entertaining video textbook. 

Thoughts?

content:
Add this sentence to every prompt if you want 10x better AI results

No comment for resource – just one sentence right below this one 👇🏽

"Ask me as many clarifying questions as you need to in order to better understand my needs and deliver better answers. Prioritize gathering information before responding to my instructions."

Why does this work? Because the best managers don’t just give orders and walk away. They leave space for questions. They want understanding before action.

With AI, you need to do the same.

Most people prompt AI like it’s a vending machine:

• “Write me an email.”
• “Give me a summary.”
• “Generate a title for my blog post.”

Then they wonder why the output feels like bland, generic AI slop 🤦🏽‍♂️

Garbage in, garbage out. 

But if you give AI a chance to ask you questions, you get gold back.

Treat AI less like a vending machine, and more like a new hire who knows *everything* but understands *nothing* about you or your goals.

You give it a task. But you don’t give it your wisdom, your context, your edge. That’s where things break.

That's where asking the AI to interview you for context creates 10x results:
• It forces AI to pause before spitting out a half-baked answer.
• It turns your prompt into a two-way street.
• It lets the AI gather the right info-like a smart teammate would.

I use this trick in almost every prompt – and using Wispr Flow to dictate my responses to my AI interviewer makes the whole process a breeze. 

Try it next time you're prompting - and tell me if you notice the upgrade!

Clay ≠ AI SDR! 

In the hyper saturated landscape of AI-GTM tech, tool categories are blurring faster than ever. But there's a timeless framework that can help us cut through the confusion: jobs to be done (JTBD).

• The JTBD of an AI SDR is 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱.
• The JTBD of Clay is 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 + 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

Cold outbound is one of 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆 data orchestration + action jobs to be done, which is where the lines get blurry. But there are 𝘁𝗼𝗻𝘀 of other use cases for Clay beyond just cold outbound.

• Generate personalized website pages for your top target accounts
• Create automatic meeting prep docs for AEs before calls
• Enrich customer data in real-time to improve CX & support 

Comparing Clay to AI SDRs is like comparing:

• Excel to budgeting apps

• Do you enrich and target product sign-ups or inbound leads?

If you're not rigorous about how you solve problems or create opportunities in your organization, you will end up in a mess of tech chaos.

Which type of GTM engineer are you? 👇🏽

There are different flavors of GTM engineering across the market, each with unique superpowers and approaches. You could be: 

🧪 The Data Alchemist - You transform raw data into golden insights. Where others see spreadsheets, you see stories waiting to be told. You're the pattern whisperer who spots trends others miss, a SQL sorcerer whose queries work like magic, and the insight generator who turns numbers into compelling narratives.

🏗️ The Automation Architect - You build systems that run themselves. Manual processes fear you, and efficiency is your middle name. You create self-running workflows, eliminate inefficiencies at scale, and literally give hours back to your teams by making growth sustainable.

🚀 The Growth Hacker - You experiment relentlessly and find unconventional paths to scale. Status quo is your enemy. You're an experiment machine always testing something new, a metric mover who makes numbers go up and to the right, and a speed demon who ships fast and learns faster.

🔍 The Revenue Detective - You investigate every lead and solve the mystery of what drives revenue. No touchpoint goes untracked. You're an attribution master who knows what really converts, a journey mapper who traces every customer path, and an ROI calculator who quantifies every investment.

🔧 The Stack Surgeon - You optimize and connect every tool with surgical precision. Your tech stack runs like a Swiss watch. You're an integration expert who connects any tools seamlessly, a stack optimizer who eliminates redundancies, and an efficiency engineer who makes everything work better.

content:
You don't burn out from working too hard. You burn out from failing.

I spent years believing burnout was about hours worked. I was wrong.

Momentum is energizing. Lack of momentum is draining.

Think about it:
• When was the last time you felt exhausted working on something that was succeeding?
• When was the last time you felt energized pushing through a project that was clearly failing?

I have nearly infinite energy for things I find interesting and that are working. And almost none for things that aren't interesting or aren't working.

This is why so many founders try something, fail, and assume they "don't have what it takes" to work hard enough.

That's rarely true.

The thing just didn't work. And that's ok.

The best advice? Shut down what's failing, take a vacation, and try again.

When you look at incredibly productive people and wonder "how do they do so much?" — they have the benefit of momentum. Success creates energy which fuels more success.

Momentum is a superpower. The trick isn't working harder — it's finding what works.

What's something in your life that energizes rather than drains you?
