content:
The B2B sales secret that nobody talks about: 

"What will I tell my boss?"

Once you've got champion buy-in, they turn into a seller. And your role shifts from selling them to *coaching them* on selling *internally*. 

If you don't arm them with the right story, you've already lost.

— 

I've seen great deals die even when they got "everything right". Better metrics, lower price, proven results.

But even the best logic loses to this one-liner: "It's what OpenAI, Anthropic, and Figma use."

Game over.

—

Here's what actually happens after you leave the room:

✅ Your champion needs to justify the purchase  
✅ Their boss needs to look smart to *their* boss  
✅ Everyone needs a story that reduces career risk

When you realize this is the pattern of buying, stories like McKinsey charging HBO $155M to go from HBO → HBO Max → Max → HBO Max over 3 years start to make sense. 

The results? Questionable.
But nobody gets fired for "hiring McKinsey". 

The best products don't always win.  
The best *stories* do.

👉 If you want to close more deals, you need to stop selling features.

Start crafting the internal pitch your champion will give when you're not in the room. 

Because if they default to "it's like what we have, but cheaper"?

You've already lost.

content:
"I just want to use what all the other sales teams are using"

One of our vendors told me that this was what one of our team members told them when we downsized our contract with them in favor of a more "market standard" tool. 

This evoked an unusually strong visceral anger emotion for me – so I took a pause to reflect on why. There were two core reasons: 

• The hypocrisy 👀. Imagine if every revenue leader said that to us. "Sorry, nobody every got fired for signing with Z***info so I'm just gonna stick with that". Clay simply wouldn't exist. 

• When this change was being floated at the company, I *explicitly* told the team that I didn't care what decision they made as long as they ensured there were no execution risks. Since we've made the switch – we've had continuous issues with the tool functionality (several people have asked me individually about it), I was assured that the AI features *had* improved, and ... they have not. In fact, we mostly just connect the data to Clay for most functional use cases ... 🤦🏽‍♂️.

But after I took a brief pause and calmed down, I realized these are *great* competitive advantages. 

• Market standard creates a layer of protection. When I was selling Clay, I actually *did* have several revenue leaders tell me "nobody every got fired for bringing on Z***info, so ....". We eventually won those companies over with a combination of persistence + superior results. Which is an important reminder to never let a brand moat dilute actual value delivered. 

• First mover advantage is real, especially because of switching costs. Varun Anand actually brought this up at our Q2 planning in regards to *another* tool that we currently use that is clearly worse for our use case than a competitor – but is good enough for the job so we're not gonna bother ripping and replacing. The pain isn't real enough. 

Some teachable insights instead for teams going up against "market standards": 

• Persistence is key, & multi-threading is important. If you're talking to an exec who just wants the market standard, find the exec who cares about "the best". 

• If you *know* your product is better – build grassroots support/champions internally. It's easy for execs to ignore outside opinions about the tech stack. Harder to ignore complaints from your own employees. 

• Find the pain that matters most. For Clay, "data" is often the entry point - but not always. If a company already has "good enough" data, we need to figure out what matters *most* to them. There's no replacement for creating (genuine) impact and urgency.

• Investing in brand pays off. Nobody becomes a "market standard" overnight. It takes years of hard work, smart marketing, killer sales, high value customer experience, and a series of high quality events to pull this off. If you're looking to overtake the market standard, start with delivering value, but you'll quickly have to evolve into competing on brand as well. 

thoughts? 🤔

content:
🍰 Cake Mix, 🌼 Origami, 🧱 Legos - what do all these products have in common? 

The IKEA effect. 

People value things MORE when they help create them.

Your customers don’t always want the “easiest possible version”. 

Sometimes, making the process *more* involved to creates ownership is better.

It's why Betty Crocker added eggs to instant cake mix, and why people will defend the wobbly IKEA shelf they built themselves till the ends of the earth. 

This happens with tech too. 

Take Notion for example. 

The blank canvas approach allows for infinite customizability. 

People build their Notion workspaces from scratch, and feel SO much pride in their work that there’s a whole marketplace just for notion templates (some people do just want that pre-baked cake!). 

Figma, Notion, Clay, and so many others are all the same. 

I call these “fat, not lean” tools. 

Figma took 3 years to launch. Notion took 5. Clay took 7. 

It’s not simple to build tools like these - they’re often labors of love from founders obsessed with the craft as opposed to the quick SaaS hit. 

This is evermore true in the era of AI, where it feels like almost everything could be made infinitely easier or automated. 

My prediction? 

Products that turn users into creators will come out on top. 

Turn the “learning curve” from a bug into a feature.

content:
AI is boosting productivity – but mostly for top performers.

Which means it’s widening the skill gap, not closing it.

🔬 An MIT study of 1,000+ R&D scientists tested an AI tool. The results?

✅ Top researchers doubled their output.
❌ The bottom third saw zero improvement.

💡 Another study gave entrepreneurs a GPT-4 “AI mentor”:

✅ High performers increased revenue ~20%.
❌ Low performers saw revenue drop ~10% 🤯.

The pattern is clear: AI rewards expertise. The more skilled you are, the more AI amplifies your output. Meanwhile, less experienced users struggle – or worse, get misled by AI’s confident wrong answers.

People fear AI replacing experts, but in practice, AI is *supercharging* them.

That means that to invest in AI adoption, you should *first* invest in core skills. Instead of throwing AI tools at your entire org, deploy them first to your top performers. Let them show you what’s possible—then train the rest.

AI isn’t just another check-the-box initiative. It’s a force multiplier—but only if you first teach people what great looks like.

content:
🔥 Take: The best path to becoming a founder (for new grads) isn't to start a company.

When I graduated college, I was obsessed with entrepreneurship. I loved the art of creating and building. 

So I did what made the most sense: I started my own thing.

I learned an *incredible* amount from that first company - but there were just as many pitfalls. 

Here's what nobody tells you about the "founder-first" path:

• You're limited by what YOU know (which isn't much when you're 22)
• You have no proven patterns to follow
• You lack a great team to bounce ideas off (even if you have great co-founders) 
• You miss the "this works, this doesn't" playbook
• You're navigating in the dark... alone

What I've come to realize is that the best founder training ground isn't founding something at all.

👉 The smarter path:

Join a rocket ship at 50-200 employees. Take ANY role that excites you.

Then do what most people don't: take on the projects & tasks that nobody is handling. At fast-growing companies with product-market fit, these opportunities are EVERYWHERE.

You're diving into entrepreneurship with training wheels:
✅ Real ambiguity and problem-solving
✅ Mentors who've been there before
✅ Resources to actually execute ideas
✅ A team to learn with and from
✅ Permission to fail without losing everything

I've seen this pattern repeatedly, and I've felt it most deeply over my last 2.5 years at Clay. In many ways, I've gotten to flex *more* founder skills at Clay than I ever have building on my own. 

When you learn the 1-100 journey FIRST—it preps you in incredible ways to eventually go to 0-1 yourself one day.

—

That is exactly why we've launched "The Wheel™" – our New Grad Rotational Program at Clay. 

We're giving ambitious graduates the chance to work across GTM, Product, and Engineering at one of the fastest-growing startups in NYC (we just hit unicorn status! 🦄).

You'll get hands-on experience solving real problems, learning from senior leaders, and building skills that would take YEARS to develop on your own.

The best part? You'll see firsthand how a rocket ship actually works—from the inside.

content:
I'm firing my VP of Sales today.

Words from a founder's mouth I've been coaching for several months. 

I'm confused, I say. He's only been here 45 days. Why are you firing him?

It's been almost two months, he hasn't made a substantial impact. He didn't close any deals last month and the team didn't close any more than before he was here. 

Puzzled, I ask what he has done since he's been here. 

We whiteboarded (shout out to Dale) everything he's done. 

↳Met the team
↳Spent time with other department leaders
↳Spent DAYS with the founder transferring knowledge
↳4 customer dinners
↳Attended his first BOD meeting
↳Shadowed sales and success calls
↳Met with existing customers to learn "why" they bought
↳Built out hiring plans and capacity models

He also had to battle with marketing who was insistent that "sales is the problem" because all of their "leads" are fantastic. 

That VP of Sales you hire is not a magic pill that produces revenue immediately. 

Sure, they should have an immediate impact (see above), but you MUST have the proper foundation in place to see revenue scale.

Don't be so quick to fire people who are doing all the right things. 

How'd the story end?

Founder took my advice and held off on firing the VP. 

6 months later, the VP is thriving in the role.

Sales are increasing.

Churn is decreasing.

All is well in the world.

content:
Will AI agents define the next era of the internet? 

Sahar Mor thinks so. In his latest blog post, Sahar predicts that AI agents will redefine web browsing much like mobile did in the 2010s when smartphones exploded.

While I'm not convinced that an agent-centric web will replace the internet as we know it, I *do* believe that the future looks more like a blend of agent-browsing + human browsing. 

My prediction? 

The parts of the internet that will *stay* human are ones reserved for creativity, connection, experience, and community. AI will affect these categories (see - Notebook LLM), but the core primitives will stay human. 

• Social media
• Digital communities
• Blogs, Newsletters, Podcasts, any creative content locus

AI Agents will take over all the digital ops you could easily outsource to a human with instructions. Manual googling + research is at the center of most of these tasks. 

We're already seeing proof of this agent-centric world with all the crazy ways Clay customers use Claygent today. With Claygent, people have set up workflows that automatically: 

• Scrape all company logos mentioned on case studies or blog posts on a website
• Research branch specific hours, information, and staff count for national franchises 
• Summarize important strategic shifts, competitive risks, and financial data from public company 10-Ks

and so much more. These Agentic workflows are replacing the dozens to hundreds of hours teams were spending *manually* copy/pasting this data from the internet. 

I'm not 100% certain what the agentic future holds for us – but I *am* 100% that we're moving quickly towards a world where data is a commodity, rather than the equivalent of digital oil. 

What's *always* mattered (and will continue to matter) is *how* people use the data available to them. 

This is turning into an essay, so instead I'll save the rest for a post tomorrow about why this isn't anything new, and why AI might be savior, not the death, of sales and marketing.

There's a few things here I'd actually clarify: 

- We don't run verification on every email, only net new emails! (so if we already invalidated an email in an earlier step, we don't actually rerun validation!) 

- It IS possible to fully validate emails. The few emails that *can't* be validated are often "catch-all" emails - and you can toggle whether or not you want to flag catch-all emails as valid in the waterfall options (you want to be careful with how you send to these emails anyways). 

the only thing worse than wasting credits in Clay is burning your emails' domain health score, and having all your emails to VALID emails go to spam 🥲

that said, my biggest recs for saving credits in clay: 

- use your own openAI key vs. clay credits for AI runs
- purchase validation credits directly through a provider instead of through Clay (the unit cost is better) 
- use HTTP/API for any cheaper integrations you find (and let us know! we'll add them to the product!) 

the email waterfall is actually probably one of the things I most recommend people use frequently in clay to maximize coverage while saving their domain health! 

and for those pesky catch-all emails, pull out the validation status, and batch your outreach <3 (or use AI to fully write personalized emails that won't get auto-rejected from those servers)

💡 Tip to save $$$ on Clay 💡

This one mistake is costing you so much credits...


When it comes to email finding:

↳ You shouldn’t use the waterfall on Clay ❌

Let me repeat.

↳ You shouldn’t use the email waterfall on Clay ❌


⚔️  Here's a little-known tactic to save even more credits

If you're using the "Clay waterfall", then every single email will go through an email validation tool (eg. Zero Bounce).

A validation column will be added for each provider and hidden by default


1°) The problem? 

↳ Every time it does this, you use 1 Clay credit.


2°) The bigger problem? 

↳ Email verification tools included in Clay (Debounce, Zerobounce etc.) are less advanced than  which means they will incorrectly classify some Findymail emails as "risky" even though they're safe to use. That is because they were unable to validate an email, but it doesn't mean it's invalid!

That means you're paying to use fewer emails than you should.


3°) The solution

↳ Unfortunately, you can't disable verification for a single provider only so instead for now I'd recommend dropping the waterfall altogether and just using the "Find Work Email via Findymail" on its own.

We have the best email coverage on the market so putting email finders after us will only get you minimal results (maybe 5% more emails maximum).

However, the email verification step above can remove you up to 20-30% valid emails (!!), so getting this back offsets wayyyyy more than the few % you're losing by not waterfalling.

And it uses a lot fewer Clay credits!

This is the best way to leverage Findymail on Clay right now.

Clay is a good tool to build your lead lists but it can quickly get expensive, that's why it can be interesting to bring your own Findymail API key to reduce the costs of finding emails 😎

content:
The rapid evolution of AI is incredibly exciting. It feels like we're expanding capabilities every other week 👀

But if you're a GTM leader, you can't onboard your team to a new tool every other week. 

So as a prospective buyer, how do you ensure that you stay on top of the most relevant tooling for your team, and bet on the right tools? 

After hundreds of conversations with GTM and Procurement leaders, I've noticed there's one characteristic that trumps all: 

Flexibility

Why? Because flexibility solves the most pressing issues facing GTM teams today: 

• More channels and more customers -> moving more data more frequently across the stack
• GTM teams need to build experiments quickly to test quickly 
• Flexible tech -> less tech and process debt 
• Tooling is changing every week -> flexible stacks allow you to integrate new tools without high switching costs 

The next wave of SaaS is all about how well you integrate into the broader ecosystem vs. having a monster solution that beats out everything else. 

Every tool you add to your tech stack should help your GTM org get more CRISP: 

• C(ollect) - How do you get initial data about customers?
• R(each) - How do you communicate with customers at scale? 
• I(ntegrate) - How do you connect data across your stack? 
• S(tore) - Where do you access customer data? 
• P(ersonalize) - How do you gain deeper insights on your customers?

Flexible tools that power multiple parts of CRISP always beat out inflexible tools that drive value across a single dimension. 

What matters most to you when you're evaluating new tech for your team?

content:
Yesterday, my dad turned 56. And it made me realize something profound.

When I was just 2 years old, my dad took a huge leap of faith. He bet on himself and went all in on starting an electronics refurbishing company.

It was a massive risk, and it meant countless late nights and weekends building the business. Growing up, I hardly saw him - he was always hustling, grinding to make his vision a reality. To this day, I've never met anyone with his relentless work ethic. He's earned every ounce of the success that's come his way over the last 25 years.

I'll be honest - as a kid, I resented not getting more quality time with my dad. But now, with the perspective of adulthood, I realize that even though he missed some tennis matches and debate tournaments, he taught me something far more valuable:

How to be a problem solver. A tinkerer. An innovator.

I was reminded of this yesterday when he called me, beaming with pride like a 10-year-old with a shiny new toy. He regaled me with his latest invention tale.

In his new Dubai warehouse, they have a spray painting station for refurbishing laptops. But the process was horribly inefficient - it wasted paint and created toxic fumes that required employees to wear masks. 

Not ideal.

But on a recent trip to China, inspiration struck when he saw a farmer using a clever water filtration system for pesticides. He wondered: could he build something similar for his spray painting operation?

So he spent late nights researching air and water filtration. He tinkered and experimented, cobbling together prototypes. When he got stuck (which was often), he turned to his new secret weapon - Google (I'm slowly getting him into ChatGPT 😉).

Two months of tireless iteration later, he had a fully functional filtration system. It recycles 50% of the paint, eliminates the need for masks, and has his employees breathing easier (literally).

Watching the proud videos he sent me, it hit me: My dad's scrappy approach to problem-solving is the same mindset I used to first automate systems at my own nonprofit using Google Sheets.

That led me to discover Zapier. Then Airtable, Notion, Phantombuster, Make, Retool, and countless other tools I've since used to build systems for hundreds of companies - including Clay!

So thank you, Dad (and Mom). For the sacrifices. For showing me that the best entrepreneurs don't need venture capital - just grit and ingenuity.

And most of all, for the countless life lessons, both obvious and hidden. You've shaped me in more ways than you know. ❤️

Here's to the tinkerers, the problem-solvers, the innovators. May we never stop building.

content:
"See? These AI emails are getting better, but they're still *obvious*." 

My friend chuckled, hit archive on the email, and turned her screen back to herself. As fate would have it, I *knew* the sender of that email. So I knew the email was 100% human. No AI. In that moment, I was finally to verbalize why I don't think AI will "kill" sales communication. 

AI *raises*, not lowers, the bar for high quality communication. 

From door to door sales to cold email – the fundamental pillars of high quality communication have always been the same: 

1. Value Prop – What are you offering? What do I get in return? Why does it matter? 
2. Relevance – Is your value prop relevant to *me*? Is the timing right? 
3. Personalization – Did you make me feel seen and heard? or was your pitch a boilerplate waste of my time? 

In the pre-AI era, you could score points on personalization to make up for lower quality value prop or relevance. 

No longer. 

AI has transformed what USED to pass as "good messaging" and relegated it to "AI spam". 

But ... great communication still remains ... great communication. 

The vehicle doesn't matter. You could be writing cold emails, dialing cold-calls, or walking door-to-door.

If you can address the pain someone is currently feeling, get them excited to dream about future solutions, and make them feel special, they will be *excited* to talk to you. 

Our ability to be excited hasn't changed – just our bar for what actually excites us. 

Yesterday, I mentioned that the rise of AI agents will turn data from "digital oil" into a commodity. By leveling the playing field, data commodification will give more people access to the tools needed to create and engage in high quality communication. 

In 2023, the only people who could afford to be creative were those blessed with the budget & resources to acquire ALL the data they needed via providers or offshore teams. 

In 2025, a small team of technical experts can use SaaS tools like Clay to get all they data they need effectively. Now, *everyone* can be creative. 

In a world everyone has access to the same data – the future belongs to those who think creatively about what they have to say, how they want to say it, and who they want to say it to.

content:
One of the most confusing parts of building Clay over the past two years has been making sense of the following feedback: 

• "This is incredibly intuitive!" 
• "This is too complex to learn..."

Here's what I've come to realize – this feedback often isn't *actually* about Clay — it's about the nature of learning something new. 

Learning any transformative tool is inherently challenging. 

Figma, Retool, Airtable, Notion, are all tools that fundamentally alter how we work – and require significant mental shifts in how we operate.  

This isn't a UX failure—it's a feature of cognitive evolution.

The real question you should be asking yourself is NOT "Is this easy to learn?" 

Instead, ask - "Will learning this significantly transform my work?"

💡 The 10x Principle
Consider Figma. For a designer creating mockups daily, the initial learning curve isn't a barrier—it's an investment in 10x capability expansion. 

The same applies to any tool that promises fundamental transformation.

The conventional product wisdom of "reduce friction at all costs" misses a crucial truth: Some friction is necessary for transformation.

🎯 A New Framework for Tool Adoption
Some other questions to consider before investing in new tooling: 
• What specific problem(s) will this solve for me?
• Will this multiply my capabilities or just incrementally improve them?
• Am I ready to invest in changing how I think about my work?

Remember that "building process" is the investment we make in inefficiency today to either reduce inefficiency in the future or augment output. 

Spend 10 hours learning a tool that saves you 5 minutes every week - you're at a loss on your time for around 2 years. 

Spend 10 hours learning a tool that saves you hours of work every week - you're net positive after your first week or two. 

---

On the Clay side, we're continuing to invest in resources like Clay University + product features to make getting started easier for everyone enrolled in that journey of transformation ✊🏽

content:
People ask me weekly, "How do I learn how to learn?"

Nobody loves my answer. 

Most people don't *actually" want to learn how to *learn*. They just want to learn how to be *good* at things. How to skip to the end. As if there's a cheat code to learning. 

There is no cheat code. 

It does not exist. 

I used to teach a 4-week workshop on ultralearning - and we spent one whole week - 25% of the course - focused on embracing (and celebrating) failure. 

Because failure is the best teacher. The best (and fastest) way to learn how to do something the right way is to deeply understand how to do it the wrong way, repeatedly. 

That's how you build muscle memory and skill. 

We're groomed by society to only do things that we're good at. To reject things that are difficult, or hard. 

Yet, what's most difficult to learn is also often the most rewarding.

Mastering Clay wasn’t just about learning a tool, it was about overcoming a fear I didn’t even realize I had. 

I was afraid of learning. 

You might be thinking that I don't love to learn, but you'd be wrong.

I love diving into new subjects and am always exploring ideas through non-fiction.

It's just that I feared I wasn't good at learning something that comes naturally.

In other words, I'd never learned to learn. 

Here's how it would normally go:
- I'd watch YouTube videos about a subject 
-  Convinced this was going to be my new life goal, I'd enroll in an online course
- Notebook in hand, I'd dive into the material
- At the first sign of resistance, I'd start losing my resolve
- Eventually, I would skip learning the course one day
- And this would turn into me never learning it again

This was the pattern when I explored JS, Python, and tons of tools for editing videos, creating websites, learning SEO, and web scraping.

But none of them stuck. 

So what changed with Clay?

For one, I need Clay to run my business because it allows me to do the work of 2-5 people. 

In other words, I had no choice but to learn it if I wanted to stay competitive. 

Secondly, it's a creative tool. 

I've always had trouble with platforms that rquire rigid adherence to structure, language, procedure, etc.

Clay's flexibility and API access makes it so that anyone can build workflows and tables that feel like a natural extension of themselves. 

For me, it's the first time in my life that I can build what I dream without needing to ask for help.

Lastly, learning Clay has strengthened my intuitive understanding of no-code and low-code automation platforms like Make, Zapier, and Airtable. 

This makes it so rewarding because I feel like a developer who's learned a language and can pick up another more easily. 

It turns out that learning isn’t about being naturally good at something. 

It’s about finding something you would feel stupid for not knowing in a year. 

And once you've set your sights on whatever your Clay is, you'll realize how much you’re capable of because you won't stop until you figure it out. 

What's something you're grateful you took the time to learn?

content:
🔄 10 years ago, seeing "Engineer" in a job title meant one thing: you needed to code.

But that's changing fast.

Look at these roles: • Solutions Engineer • GTM Engineer • Prompt Engineer • Developer Relations Engineer • Sales Engineer

None of these jobs require traditional programming skills. But they’re still “engineers”.

Why? 

Because our definition of "technical" has evolved. Our vocabulary needs to change with it. One way we could expand the ways in which we talk about the technical fluency spectrum: 

1️⃣ Systems Technicality - (Systems designers and prompt engineers)

• Ability to think programmatically
• Understand complex systems
• Design scalable solutions

2️⃣ Tools Technicality - (The new era of no-code/low-code experts) 

• Ability to quickly master new no-code/low-code tools
• Build automated workflows
• Orchestrate tools together for maximum output

3️⃣ Code Technicality - (What we’ve always considered “technical”)

• Ability to write fully functional code
• Software development
• Technical architecture

Being "technical" in 2025 is no longer binary. 

Technicality exists along a spectrum from ways to think, tools to use, and ability to program. 

That said, I strongly believe that anyone working in a technical capacity should learn the basics of programming. It makes skill acquisition along the technical fluency spectrum far easier, no matter where you fall.

content:
not all feedback is a gift 🎁

most advice about giving feedback misses the point entirely.

traditional frameworks obsess over *how* to say things, but forget about the *why* and *what* behind our feedback.

three principles for mastering the art of feedback: 

1️⃣ start with curiosity
curiosity gets forgotten, but it's the easiest place to start. when you approach a conversation with humility - you might be surprised by what you learn. you'll also be surprised at how much more receptive people are to your feedback when they feel heard. 

❌ "I have some feedback for you" 
✅ "how do you feel about your sales performance this quarter?"

2️⃣ make it collaborative
this is the most common mistake I see. remember: feedback isn't about throwing information at someone - it's about helping them improve. reminding people that you're *literally* on their team, and there to help them makes a world of difference in creating the space for effective feedback. 

❌ "your management style makes me nervous"
✅ "I have some concerns about your management style - let's figure it out together"

3️⃣ be specific & actionable
if your feedback isn't specific, 99% of the time, you shouldn't give it. you're at risk of projecting your *feelings about* someone's work onto their *actual performance*. that won't help them them or you. unspecific feedback also risks coming across as a personal attack instead of constructive criticism. 

❌ "your output doesn't feel good enough"
✅ "your close rate on deals went down ~25% over the last quarter – how can I help?"

p.s - all the ❌'s are *real* quotes of actual feedback I've gotten! 
p.p.s - more tomorrow on how to manage up and when you get ❌ feedback instead of ✅ feedback 😅

#leadership #management #communication #feedback

---- September 2016: 

I had spent 2 weeks in React/Python/Django coding a custom ATS for the nonprofit Andy Page and I were running. Google Forms was no longer cutting it. Applications had 10-xed and our process was breaking. 

While trying to debug a regular expression – Andy told me about Zapier and Airtable. 

In just 2 days, I built the entire ATS with Zapier, Airtable, and some custom code.

My mind was blown 🤯

I dreamt of a world in which *everyone* could "code" – and build their ideas in just days. It would unlock human potential at incredible scale. 

---- September 2020:

I had a low-code automation side hustle – building custom solutions for painful processes. One recurring use case kept coming up: 

Prospecting, Enrichment, and Research. 

Every sales team was manually searching across LinkedIn, uploading lists to Hunter.io and ZoomInfo, and manually researching. It took whole days to do. 

So I built a custom-solution with Airtable, Zapier, Phantombuster, Hunter.io, DropContact, and SERP API that enabled teams to upload a SalesNav search with their LinkedIn cookie, and then returned an enriched + researched list in 30-40 minutes. 

It was a huge hit. 

---- March 2022:

Varun Anand asks me if I could replace my custom system this new tool he was jazzed about – Clay. 

I tried ... and said no. It was missing too many features.

Couldn't prospect. No phantombuster integration. The formulas were all javascript code – which my team was not well-versed in. 

But Varun was persistent. He listened to all my feedback and then some. We rebuilt the entire GTM system at Volley, and Clay became the centerpiece. 

---- January 2023: 

I took a risk and turned down a dream job at Zapier to join Clay full-time. It was less than a dozen people working out of an apartment in Williamsburg, but I thought it would be a more fun adventure. 

Worst come to worst, I could go back to Zapier or somewhere similar if it all went kaput. 

---- January 2025 

Clay has exploded. It's my two year anniversary. 

Today, we're celebrating becoming an official "unicorn", but we're just getting started. 

What I've loved most about the journey has been witnessing the massive unlock of human potential. 

When people *really* learn how to use Clay, they get GTM superpowers. It's the secret weapon of companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Rippling.

Clay is a GTM Development Environment. 

A place where anyone from the GTM team can "code" up their wildest, most creative plays without needing to build an entire app from scratch. 

There's nothing like Clay on the market – BUT, there's still tons of small bugs that we can dramatically improve. We have some crazy functionality planned for this year. And we're going to make it *way* easier to learn. 

We're just getting started 😤

You're using Slack wrong. 99% of people use Slack the way a baby plays with a bead maze— fumbling through messages haphazardly.

🦸🏽‍♂️ Make Slack a superpower, not a curse.

People are barely able to keep up on their own messages, let alone keep a finger on the pulse of the entire company.

There's a better way. 

🚫 Stop using your mouse 
✅ Start using keyboard shortcuts

Now, Slack has 100+ keyboard shortcuts. Overwhelming 🥵

The good news – you only need 10 shortcuts to unlock this superpower: 

1. ⌘ + K → quick switcher, your best friend for catching up
2. ⌘ + [ or ] → move back + forward in conversation history 
3. ⌘ + . → toggle sidebar for threads
4. ⌘ + G  → search messages *in* the current channel
5. ⌘ + F → search messages across your worspace 
6. ↑ + ↓ → move up/down messages in a channel, and then:  
7. ‘r’ → instantly add emoji reactions
8. 'e' → edit a message
9. ‘t’ → jump into threads
10. 'm' → snooze important messages 

The result? I never touch my mouse in Slack. Staying keyboard first allows me to: 
	•	Stay relevant with all product changes and new workflows
	•	Connect dots across product, eng, sales, marketing, and CX
	•	Make higher quality, faster decisions

In a hyper-growth environment, information is currency. Don’t let it slip through your fingers.

content:
I have never had to block anyone on LinkedIn ... until today. 

Interactions like this are what give sales people a bad rep. 

This doesn't even have the messages dating all the way back to Sept 12th, when I was initially cold messaged. 

After a quick look at the product, I kindly said "not interested".

I've spent a fair bit of time in Sales - and I respected the hustle, so I gave them a little more context on why we weren't a good fit. 

But they didn't listen. 

Even *if* the product would be game-changing for me or our team, I now have a *horrible* association with it. 

Sales reps - remember that your job is *not* about shilling products. 

It's about building relationships.

Small details that would have yielded a very different outcome: 
• Do your research. Clay doesn't have sales people, we have GTM engineers. Look at our careers page. 

• If someone asks for materials/use cases, they're giving you a *chance*. Don't ignore them and keep reciting your script. Meet people where they need to be met.

• You have to *earn* the right to pitch. Ask more specific questions. I glanced at this company's website, and any of the following questions would have led to a lot more learning + back-and-forth (knowing what tools we use): 


• How does your team currently search for information across Slack, Google Drive, notion, and your other tools? 
• How often do you use Notion AI to find resources? How often do you actually get the right answer?
• How do GTM engineers prep and find all the materials they need for calls when they're on back to back meetings? 

non-leading, SPIN style questions that could have led them to tailor more customized follow-ups. 

even if you do it all right, you're not guaranteed interest. 

you're *never* guaranteed interest. 

learning when to stop is just as important as learning when to keep pushing. 

#sales #relationships #discovery

Here's my cold outreach process that drives about a 17% response rate:

STEP1: Review my Linkedin Sales Nav "Tier1" saved search with specific criteria on my exact ICP.  Find someone new who has been added to the list. 
 
STEP2: Review their profile to see if they have posted anything meaningful in the past month.  If they have, make a meaningful comment on the post (NOT just a 'like' or 'great post' or 🔥). 

STEP3: Send a connection request without personalizing (getting a 3x higher acceptance rate when I don't personalize) 

STEP4: Add them to my Clay table to streamline my research for them and find out everything I need to know and all the "triggers" (I'll share the link to a post I did previously about Clay in the comments. Full disclosure, Clay is a sponsor of mine but only because I f-ing love their platform and it makes me 10x more efficient with my research)

STEP5: Identify a few 'triggers' I can use to send a personalized e-mail to the contact. 

STEP6: take the "double tap" approach and make a call (usually leave a voicemail) to the contact referencing the email.

STEP7: go back on Linkedin to see if they accepted my request.

STEP8: find another trigger (on Linkedin) that I can connect to (usually for me it's something like hiring or a super relevant post) and send them a video or voice message on Linkedin (can only do on mobile devices).

What's your most effective sequence/cadence these days?

repost.content:
"be the last mile"

I've figured out the line (for me) when it comes to engaging with AI related to Sales and content.

I have no problem reading or consuming content created by AI as long as I know it's coming from AI. 

BUT, if someone uses AI to create content and then pretends like it was created by a human (emails, linkedin posts/comments, chat bots, etc) and I can sense that it was, I don't care how good the content is, I immediately discredit it.

It's like the early days of chatbots.  Remember when you first engaged with a chatbot on a website and it pretended to be a human?

At first, you were like "wow, this person is so responsive and helpful."

But then, after the 3rd or 4th chat you realized it wasn't a human? 

I don't know about you but as soon as I got that sense, I got annoyed and started typing in "live agent" until I got one.

But then Drift came out with their chatbot and when you were on a site it said "I'm not a human but I can help get you the majority of answers you need. What can I help you with?"

I was fully engaged and enjoyed the experience after that.

It's the same with posts on Linkedin, comments, blogs, emails, etc.  

We're still in a place with AI where I can sense that content is written by AI.

When that happens, and you pretend like it is, you lose credibility in my eyes.

This is why "human as the last mile" is so critical. 

I met with Gary Vaynerchuk back in 2017 when I had seen an AI bot write a personalized email better and faster than I ever could and asked him where that leaves us as humans.

He said something that sticks with me to this day which was: "don't worry about the tech, you're not going to beat it.  Be the last mile. Let it do all the heavy lifting but right before you hit send make sure you humanize it.  Because, as long as there is a human on the other end of that message, there will be a need for that human touch."

That's why I talk about augmentation, NOT automation with AI.  

I have no problem with AI doing all the research (see my post last week about what I'm doing with Clay from a prospecting perspective). 

I don't even mind using AI to write the email, post or comment to get the idea flow going.

BUT, if you then just cut/paste/send and don't then humanize it then what is the point of you as a sales professional?  What value do you add?

If you're answer is - "look at how much more efficient I am than other reps" then congrats, you just automated your job and I don't need you any more. 

Using AI as a copilot to generate ideas and do the heavy lifting is smart. 

Using AI to automate your outreach, posts, comments, follow up etc is just feeding into your/our unemployment.

Be the last mile.

content:
🎯 The hardest word for leaders to say? 

“No.”

I watched hundreds of leaders struggle with this in my work as a coach. 

Avoiding a tough conversation makes things feel rosy for a few weeks, or months. 

But it's an implicit lie. An unclear "no" almost always gets heard as an "okay"

long-term, implicit lies breed mistrust, resentment, and will lead to your best people being deeply dissatisfied.

Here’s the truth:
Avoiding tough conversations doesn’t protect your team—it damages them.

Why do people struggle to say “no”?
🤔 Fear of conflict
😟 Desire to be liked
🌪️ Hope that issues will resolve themselves

But here’s what REALLY happens when you dodge saying “no”:
❌ Trust erodes
❌ Expectations become misaligned
❌ Resentment builds silently

Tough as it is - a clear “no” builds MORE trust long-term than an unclear “maybe.”

But, you also can't JUST say "no" and expect things to go well. 

3 keys to mastering the art of “no”:
💡 Listen deeply, integrate your team's perspective.
💪 Explain your reasoning clearly.
🤝 Acknowledge ambiguity when present, and promise to course-correct if needed.

Great leadership isn’t about making your team happy—it’s about making your team *feel heard*.

What’s your experience with saying “no”? 

#Leadership #Management #CorporateCulture #PersonalDevelopment

Attention 10x’d from from mid-6 to mid-7 figure ARR in a year. 
Here’s how they did it:

1/ Solve your own problem

Anis Bennaceur  and Matthias Wickenburg, the co-founders of Attention, both had experienced the pain of keeping Salesforce updated at their previous startups. 
That’s why they built Attention - originally a tool that automatically updates CRMs after calls.
Today, they’ve expanded the feature set massively, from drafting follow-up emails, to real-time coaching.
But first, they started by solving their own problem.

2/ Have the right timing

Attention was founded in 2021, right as LLM performance started to take-off.
This was perfect timing in terms of market entrance. 
Production ready LLMs meant sophisticated AI software was possible. 
Attention had all the tools in place to build a modern, AI-first replacement for a antiquated industry.

3/ Build differentiators in-house, use vendors to build commodity features

Attention knew they had to move fast to keep up with the pace of innovation in the AI space. 
To do this, they focused all their time on building out their differentiating features, while using vendors for commoditized parts of their stack, such as the sales call recording and transcription features.

They effectively delegated their time to figure out what was needed to built vs bought.

It wasn’t about cutting corners. It was about scaling smarter.

At Recall.ai , we’re honored to be powering Attention’s sales call recording feature. 

Time is your most valuable resource. If you’re starting a company, pick a problem you already know deeply, understand the “why now?” and execute as fast as possible. 🚀

content:
Experience is the best teacher.

Or is it?

Experience is a seductive teacher.

Personal. Visceral. Real.

But experience is only half the story. 

In our haste to learn from experience, we weigh our own experiences more heavily than we should. Each success becomes a story. Every failure hardens into a rule.   The lessons we “learn” from experience draw invisible boundaries around our thinking.

The founder who succeeded through persistence tells everyone to never give up. The one who pivoted early preaches rapid adaptation. Both miss the larger truth: they're looking at the world through a keyhole of their own making.

Experience is availability bias dressed up as wisdom.

The more experience we gain, the more we trust our judgment. 
The more we believe we know. 
The more we stop questioning. 
The more we stop seeing alternatives.

And that's precisely when experience becomes dangerous - when it transforms from a teacher into a cage.

Real wisdom isn't about collecting experiences.

It's about developing the intellectual courage to challenge them.

Two questions that can transform how you reflect on your experiences:
• What's missing? 
• What's irrelevant?

“Experience isn’t the best teacher. Evaluated experience is.” - John C. Maxwell

🔥 take - everyone is getting the whole GTME vs. RevOps debate wrong. 

It’s NOT GTM Engineering OR RevOps.
It’s GTM Engineering AND RevOps.

Here’s why:

👉 RevOps keeps the machine running at optimum performance.

Enrichment flows? Email sequences? CRM integrations? RevOps keeps them all running smooth and flawless.

RevOps ensures the plane is well maintained, properly-tuned, and flying without danger of crashing. 

RevOps is the backbone of consistent, effective execution that fosters reliable growth. 

👉 GTM Engineers are mad-scientists in a growth lab.

GTMEs are the ones pushing boundaries, experimenting with cutting-edge strategies—like LLM-driven personalized outreach, automated follow-ups, and enrichment workflows that eliminate manual effort.

The growth strategies that work today won't be the same as what works next quarter. Your customers are constantly changing, and your growth strategies adapt with them.

GTMEs are your constant 0-1 experimentation hit-team. They make things work ⚒️
RevOps are your 1-100 scaling experts. They make things great 🚀

Without scaling, you’re leaving opportunities on the table. Without experimentation, you’re risking irrelevance.

GTME AND RevOps -> 1 + 1 = 100 
GTME OR RevOps -> 1 | 1 = 1 

Choice is yours 😉

content:
alright, I've asked 4 different people this question today and got very strong opinions on totally different sides of the spectrum. 

so I'm curious what you all think.

first, what everyone universally agrees on: 

• outbound email is a form of marketing sent to customers or potential customers who *did not opt in* to communication. (e.g - cold email sequences)

• inbound email is a form of marketing sent to people who *did opt in* to communication about your product. (e.g - free trial email sequences)

now, enter the gray area. if you send emails to customers who have been using the product for 3-6 months, based on behavior taken in the product, with the goal of upselling them, do you consider that outbound or inbound? 

or something else entirely?

leave any nuance in comments 👇🏽 I'll drop my own opinion too

If you're not using AI to write AI prompts, you're wasting time.

A couple months ago, Yash Tekriwal from Clay put this on my radar during a ColdIQ live session.

If you go to the Anthropic dashboard, the second option you'll see is "Generate a prompt".

Here's what I asked Claude to create one of my most useful prompts:

"I want you to normalize a company name:

{{company name}}

Max Length is 2 words, but a 3 word output is permitted if necessary. Cut out pointless words to leave the most unique descriptors. 

For example if Company is Agilent Technologies, you can do Agilent. If Company name is Career Search International, you can put CSI. 

Countries should mostly be removed, for example Generali Switzerland should be outputted as Generali.

But the leftover word should not be overtly general. 

For example, Health New England should remain as is since "Health" isn't unique enough as a word."

-----

Since implementing this tool, I spend way less time writing prompts.

And my output quality has improved.

I've read countless guides on how to prompt AI optimally.

Just to realize, AI can do this for me.

Now I just tell Claude what I want to achieve.

content:
"A jack of all trades is a master of none ...." 

Did you know that's only half the quote? 🤔

" ... though oftentimes better than a master of one." 🤹🏽‍♂️

I was shocked the first time I heard this. Growing up, I was constantly told that I needed to "focus" my talents into ONE thing that would lead to a fruitful career. 

Conventional wisdom tells us that you can't be *really* good at multiple things, so you should be the *best in the world* at just one. 

Career-wise, I believe this was more true in the pre-software era. 

But the advent of software has massively lowered the learning curve required to ramp up new skills.

AI is 10xing that curve. 

30 years ago, it made no sense for me to entertain working on design projects. I'd have to learn how to properly draw, shoot, film, edit, and so much more. 

Then Photoshop was created in 1987. Canva in 2013. Now DALL-E, Sora, and so much more with AI. 

At each step, the answer to, "should I invest the time to learn and do this myself?" becomes "yes" for more and more people. 

The kicker is that the best generalists I've ever met are now specialists in their own right. When you enter the 90th percentile for multiple skills, you become part of the *very* small group of people who are able to weave together and connect skills across seemingly disparate functions in the world. 

This is all I could think about this morning when I started using Sora. Before today, I would have had to hire a video editor, sink hours into learning video editing, or likely some combination of all the above.

It would have taken weeks. 

This took 15 minutes of prompting, some storyboarding, and iterating. 

It's an incredible time to be a generalist. Someone who can think creatively, implement quickly, and build with precision. 

And we're just getting started. 

Happy holidays everyone.

when you're selling or supporting a complex product, it's easy to get lost in the weeds with customers.

a story from a call this week: 

"can you please try to understand what I'm asking you, and then answer again" - Customer

the rep was taken aback. he had *just* answered the question. I can confirm that his answer was 100% accurate. but the customer still didn't "get it" 😕

because the problem wasn't the answer. it was the *delivery*.

nobody understands this problem better than teachers. being understood is far harder than being correct.

when I taught high school, I had to come up with a million different ways to explain the same concept. 

not because the first explanation was wrong. but because different students have different backgrounds, and different ways of seeing the world.

that doesn't change after graduation. 

the art of working with customers isn't about transferring knowledge – it's about transforming understanding.

content:
The "Blank Canvas" is the biggest blocker new users face when getting started in Clay.

It's like writer's block. You're staring at a blank table, and, all of a sudden, your brain goes just as blank as the table in front of you. 

Where do you start? 
What are you trying to accomplish? 
Are you just about to waste your whole day fumbling around this blank canvas? 

After hopping on calls with hundreds of customers, I've developed a simple framework that helps people wrap their heads quickly around Clay: FETE. 

• Find
• Enrich
• Transform
• Export 

No matter what your use case is (inbound, outbound, CRM enrichment, or something else), you're following the FETE framework. You always need to Find data to start with, you always Enrich that data to get a more clear picture, then you Transform it to be formatted in the way that suits your team best, before Exporting it to it's final resting place (often a CRM or email sequencer).

We've gotten so much positive feedback on FETE that it's the foundational framework we give to every student at the beginning of the Clay 101 intro video on ClayU. 

Do you have any mental models you use for how you approach workflow building in Clay?

We expect each of our BDRs to generate 30-40 SQLs per month on month 4.

When stress testing this with brilliant sales leaders, they all asked me “how on earth?”

So far, Rory and Jake are crushing their numbers without running any automated sequences.

Here’s how we did it (and how you should do it too):

1️⃣ Boost confidence: set the very first objective to be 1 SQL in their first 48 hours on the job.
We had an internal contest: 1st one to get his sql gets $150.
If both do, each gets $200.
Getting that first sql and going from zero to one changes everything for them.
Because once you taste success, you will know how to repeat that.

2️⃣ Startups principles and marketing 101: We blocked a full hour to teach our first principles as a startup, and the need to always create urgency + our intolerance for misexecution.
And also the concepts of adoption curve and intent.
This deeply informs the why behind everything that they do.
Both Jake and Rory had already read every single Paul Graham essay and Amp it up by Frank Slootman before starting.

3️⃣ Be technical AND excellent hunters: in addition to the traditional BDR training they got, they also immediately learned everything about our internal intent infrastructure and how to use Clay and CaptainData to keep enriching it.
